en: Preface to the Treatise on the Eight Consciousnesses:

Regarding the fundamental principle of the Sage’s essence and function, there are the two gateways of Nature (svabhāva) and Characteristics (lakṣaṇa). Now, as for these two gates of Nature and Characteristics...
This means that within the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), there is both a gate of arising and ceasing and a gate of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Now, the gate of arising and ceasing refers to the mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*) of the School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*).

The gate of non-arising and non-ceasing refers to the principle of the empty essence of the School of Nature (*dharmatā-yāna*). Thus, there are no characteristics apart from nature, and no nature apart from characteristics. Therefore, within the gate of *tathatā*, [arising and ceasing...]
It is the very essence of the Dharma-body, which is no different from that which is neither born nor extinguished. Since there is no distinct essence, when encountering objects, clarity is manifest.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature and characteristics, it is said: "Mind-only, no external objects. If there are no objects, from whom would the self-mind arise?
Thus, mind and objects vanish into one another; all is vast and empty, beyond the reach of sagehood. It manifests the Great Image, yet its form remains unseen.
It is utterly vast like empty space, yet its form cannot be seen. Therefore, it is not bright above, nor is it obscure below.
It encompasses heaven and earth in its greatness, yet enters into a single mote of dust in its subtlety. It is neither form nor emptiness; it is neither wisdom nor consciousness.
Because the five eyes cannot perceive its shape, even the four types of eloquence cannot describe its appearance. Thus, it is continuous and beyond naming—quiescent.

It is quiescent and invisible. One cannot see its head when approaching it; one cannot see its rear when following it. The more one drills into it, the firmer it becomes; the more one probes it, the less trace it leaves.
Subtle, wondrous, and profoundly penetrating, it is deep and beyond comprehension. It is so rarefied and ethereal that all signs of it vanish; it is ultimately unknowable.
(Alas! One can only harmonize this within the mind and accord with it through the spirit. It serves as the progenitor of the Tripiṭaka and the fundamental principle of the Ten Stages.
Those who are deluded transform the nature of wisdom into consciousness and form; those who awaken transform consciousness and form back into the nature of wisdom.
When form and consciousness are established, the six realms of existence manifest together; when the nature of wisdom is established, even illusory existence is simultaneously transcended.
Quiescence. Furthermore, when both are manifested, the sovereign mind of the *ālayavijñāna* is perfected; when both are quiescent, the forms and substances of the myriad phenomena are discarded.

Moreover, when the sovereign mind arises, the various distractions of love and hatred follow; when the *ālayavijñāna* is empty, the incessant breaths of the *pravṛttivijñānas* of ignorance are shattered.
If one can penetrate the true principle of *vijñaptimātra* and realize the non-existence of the *dharmatā*, [one attains liberation].
As for the subject matter, it would not bring shame upon those who study the Dharma. However, I am personally ashamed of my own lack of insight;
having failed to enter the hall to inquire into the profound mystery, I have exhausted my thoughts without end.
Thus, I truly pray for the secret empowerment of the Sage and sincerely knock at the gate.

With reverence, we prostrate ourselves before the Buddha Maitreya; As if the Honored One were present before our eyes, Though the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Today, having no one from whom to seek further instruction, I pray for the power of hidden grace.
I have taken up the brush to compose this treatise, exhausting the essential principles of the eight consciousnesses. Every word accords with the intent of the Patriarchs;

May it universally benefit all ordinary beings, so that they may together realize the nature of *vijñapti-mātratā*. By means of these pure, wondrous, and wholesome merits, I dedicate them toward the Pure Land.
May one swiftly behold Amitābha and suddenly cast off all karmic retribution.
Regarding the present mention of the "eight consciousnesses": when the One is dispersed, it becomes the myriad differences; thus it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
When the myriad differences are unified as the One, what is here termed "consciousness-only" is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*. This is because there are no phenomena apart from the mind.
Furthermore, "only" (wei) means that it is not accomplished by another; it is produced solely by my *ālayavijñāna*. Moreover, "only" means "accomplished.

That is to say, the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), the physical world (*bhājana-loka*), as well as the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), are all subsumed within the *ālayavijñāna* and are thus accomplished independently.
Therefore, one asks: why is it accomplished independently and not through the power of another?
Answer: It is like a person who has fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), who sees water as pus and blood, or it transforms into fire.
Thus, when Maudgalyāyana sent food to rescue his mother, it turned into burning embers. To devas and humans, water appears as lapis lazuli, while to fish, it becomes their dwelling place.
Furthermore, Sudhana visited King Mahāprabha. Beings within the city saw this city in various ways: some saw it as if made of lapis lazuli;
some saw it within as being composed entirely of the seven treasures; and others saw it within as being of sand, earth, wood, and thatched huts.
Is this not indeed the manifestation of the karmic power of the mind alone, appearing differently according to each individual? Therefore, it is the karma of one's own mind.
Because their power is strong, they perceive various distinct things; it is not that there are visible forms existing outside the mind, for [perception] follows one's own mind.
Why is this? Because the seeds of the karmic power of each person’s own mind are strong. It is like hungry ghosts who dwell together in the same place.
Since they do not see one another, it is as if they were in the same room; because each has formed their own dream, this is precisely the mind.
This applies generally to the "mind-only" nature of ordinary sentient beings. However, within the state of Buddhahood, it becomes the Great Luminous Treasury;
this pure white consciousness is named Vairocana Buddha.
Regarding what is called the "eight consciousnesses," they all belong to the category of mental factors (*caitta*) and are not [independent] mind-states (*citta*).

As for the eight consciousnesses: first, eye-consciousness; second, ear-consciousness; third, nose-consciousness; fourth, tongue-consciousness; fifth, body-consciousness; sixth, mental consciousness; seventh, *manas*-consciousness; and eighth, *ālaya*-consciousness.
Now, these consciousnesses originally have no different names; it is because their functions and spheres of activity are each distinct that they are designated as such.

Regarding "possessing number" (*saṃkhyā-sahita*): this refers to an etymological explanation based on number. When we now speak of the "five consciousnesses," they receive their names based upon their respective faculties.

Because it receives its name based on the eye, it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣur-vijñāna*); likewise, because it receives its name based on the body, it is called "body-consciousness" (*kāya-vijñāna*).

This is an example of a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. Furthermore, the eye is not the ear, and so forth, up to the ear is not the body-consciousness; this is an example of a *dvandva* (copulative) compound.
It is also called *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound). It is explained as such because the sense organ, being weak, sees only by relying upon consciousness;

thus it is termed a *tatpuruṣa*, just as a father is called "the powerful one" by relying upon his son. It is also called *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound), for consciousness is the dependent (*āśrayin*) and the sense organ is the basis (*āśraya*).

Therefore, it is called *tatpuruṣa* (dependent designation), and it is also termed *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound). This is explained within the context of the six, seven, and eight consciousnesses.
Because the Great Master Xuanzang first brought forth the forty-eight verses of the "Mother" of the Eight Consciousnesses, they are divided into four sections for exposition.
Section One: The Five Consciousnesses Transforming into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (12 Verses) Section Two:
The Six Consciousnesses Transforming into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (12 Verses) Section Three:
The Seventh Consciousness Transforming into the Wisdom of Equality (12 Verses)
Section Four: The Transformation of the Eight Consciousnesses into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. This section consists of twelve verses.
Within the four sections, the chapter on the five consciousnesses first comprises twelve verses.
These are further divided into two parts: the first eight verses constitute the Chapter on Ordinary Sentient Beings, and the latter four verses constitute the Chapter on the Holy Fruit.
The first verse:
The nature and objects of ordinary consciousness are perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and comprise all three natures;

they reside in the three [realms] of eye, ear, and body, and consist of the five universal, the five object-specific, and eleven wholesome mental factors, along with the two intermediate [unwholesome] factors, the eight great [afflictions], and greed, hatred, and delusion.

The five consciousnesses share the same support in the translucent material sense organs; they arise through nine conditions, seven or eight [conditions] respectively, with the favorable [faculties] adjacent to one another.

Three are associated with two [mental factors], while observing the world of objects. It is difficult for the ignorant to distinguish between consciousness and the faculties. Now, regarding the first of the eight statements in this treatise, it says: [Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a verse concerning the *pañcavijñānakāya* (five sensory consciousnesses) and their relationship to the *indriyas* (faculties) and *ālambanas* (objects). The translation reflects the structure and content of the original verse.]

Regarding the statement that "the objective realm of nature (svabhāva-viṣaya) and direct perception (pratyakṣa) pertain to all three natures," the treatise asks: "How is it that the objective realm of nature and direct perception pertain to all three natures? The answer is: "That which is called the 'objective realm of nature'..."
That which is immutable is its *xing* (nature). That which corresponds to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) is its *jing* (object).
This taking of nature as object refers to earth, water, fire, and wind; these four great elements constitute its nature and its object.
Question: What is meant by "immutable nature"? Answer: Earth has solidity as its nature; water has moisture as its nature; fire has... [heat].
Heat has warmth as its nature; wind has motion as its nature.

As for why each of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is said to have a "nature," it is because, just as fire cannot possibly become cool, wind cannot possibly become still. The latter two meanings can be understood accordingly;

thus, it is said that their natures are unchangeable. Furthermore, the four great elements each pervade everywhere, being neither deficient nor redundant; therefore, they are called the "four great elements."

Furthermore, they can produce [the objects]: sound, odor, taste, and touch constitute their four subtle elements (*anu*). These are the eight dharmas consisting of the [four] faculties and their [four] objects, collectively termed "form" (*rūpa*).

Sound, odor, taste, and touch are called the "four subtle elements" because they are derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). As for the term "form," it refers to that which possesses the four subtle elements.

These constitute the objective spheres (*viṣaya*) of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). They encompass everything from the internal body of the faculties (*indriya-kāya*) and the external world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*), down to light and darkness, manifest colors, and so forth;

as well as shapes such as square or round, and manifest forms (*vijñapti-rūpa*) such as walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. All these are the direct and indirect object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
This is the nature of the resultant retribution-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) which maintains them. All of this is subsumed within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
Because it is an object of perception that appears as an objective referent (*ālambana*), it is produced from the seeds of the two aspects—the seeing and the perceived.

If one has not yet destroyed the ignorance that deludes regarding the nature [of reality], it is subsumed under the nature of universal imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). If one has destroyed that delusion regarding the nature, [it is subsumed under the dependent nature].

This refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). Although it appears as if it exists, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-existent, because that which resembles the dependent nature is itself the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifesting, for it is neither past nor future; it is also like the light of a mirror. "Perception" (*pramāṇa*) means measuring;
it is the mind in its initial encounter with an object, like a mirror reflecting an image, for it does not retain any emotional attachment. It manifests like a reflected image.

Their magnitude is like the radiance of a mirror. Furthermore, the two aspects—the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga)—each have their own seeds within the seeds of the eight consciousnesses;
they arise simultaneously because there is no distinction between prior and posterior limits.
Regarding the statement that "it permeates the three natures": first, the nature of goodness; second, the nature of evil; and third, the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

What is called "nature" here refers to the seeds (*bīja*). Within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), since beginningless time, the seeds of the nature of goodness, the seeds of the nature of evil, and the seeds of the nature of the indeterminate—having been perfumed (*vāsita*)—are each fixed by their respective natures and can never be altered, much like sandalwood.

Fragrance and stinking garlic are certainly distinct by nature; therefore, among the objects of touch, if a sudden mental state (*sater-icitta*) arises—such as when a wicked person strikes a bird—it constitutes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for that single moment.
Once it falls into the sphere of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it becomes inference (*anumāna*).

If it draws forth seeds of a virtuous nature, it gives rise to thoughts of compassion and constitutes a wholesome manifest action (*kuśala-saṃskāra*); [whereas] seeds of a non-virtuous nature... [are touched].

The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) constitute the objective sphere of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When they fall within the scope of inferential consciousness (*anumāna-manovijñāna*), they give rise to the active manifestation of evil.
This applies equally to the arising of wholesome thoughts of sympathetic joy as it does to unwholesome thoughts; therefore, they are called "objective spheres" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

Because they constitute direct perception while simultaneously constituting inference, they encompass all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate natures. Thus, various types of active manifestations arise, and so forth.

Within the sphere of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-viṣaya*), one encounters the ten wholesome objects, which are accessible through both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Alternatively, one encounters the ten unwholesome objects, which are likewise accessible through both direct perception and inference.

If there were originally no seeds of the wholesome or the unwholesome, then encountering wholesome objects would not give rise to the wholesome, nor would encountering unwholesome objects give rise to the unwholesome.
Since there are no manifest seeds of either the wholesome or the unwholesome, these are termed "indeterminate seeds" (*avyākṛta-bīja*). Now, within the seven consciousnesses:
The active manifestation of good and evil perfumes the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), thereby forming the seeds of propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) among the eight consciousnesses.

These are transferred to the future, where they will inevitably result in the fruits of suffering or happiness according to whether they were good or evil. This is precisely what constitutes the "ripened fruit" (*vipāka-phala*) of the future.
Therefore, it is said that they pervade the causes and effects of the three natures; there is certainly no discrepancy.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Treatise) concerning the three—eye, ear, and body—that they "dwell in two stages":
how is it that the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body pertain only to the First Dhyāna and the Second Dhyāna heavens? That is to say:
Does this not apply to the gods of the three and four dhyānas in the higher realms? Answer:

In the lower Desire Realm (kāmadhātu), within the ground where the five destinies dwell together, all eight consciousnesses are fully present. In the gods of the First and Second Dhyānas, there is no Desire Realm;

because they have abandoned the consumption of physical food (kavaḍīkārāhāra), there are no objects of smell or taste. Thus, in these two stages, there are only six consciousnesses: first, eye-consciousness; second, ear-consciousness.
The three bodies-consciousnesses; fourth, the mental consciousness; fifth, the manas-consciousness; and sixth, the ālaya-consciousness.

Furthermore, the reason the first dhyāna possesses six consciousnesses is that, having abandoned the desire realm, one gives rise to the joy of the first dhyāna and also attains pure and sublime bliss.

How much more so for those with both vitarka and vicāra, who constantly emerge from meditative absorption to preach the Dharma for the benefit of the Brahmā devas and the devas of the second dhyāna, the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Although these latter beings lack vitarka and vicāra, they possess a mind of joy; this is called the stage of "joy born of concentration" (samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi).
Because they have attained deep concentration and possess a joyful mind, even though they do not constantly emerge from absorption, they manifest preaching the Dharma within their radiance.
Because there is sound, the various Brahma assemblies also possess the objects of the three consciousnesses—eye, ear, and body.

Thus, it is credible that those who dwell in the two lower stages [of the form realm] possess the three: eye, ear, and body. Furthermore, it was asked: "In the first and second dhyānas, can the two mental factors of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) exist?
The answer is: "Before entering meditative absorption in the first dhyāna, both *vitarka* and *vicāra* exist; after having entered absorption, only *vicāra* remains."

There is no *vitarka* (applied thought). In the second dhyāna, there is only *vicāra* (sustained thought) and no *vitarka*. Since there is joy and bliss in the mind, how could *vicāra* be absent? Again, he asked:
"In the third dhyāna, can the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body exist? He replied: "Only while in meditative absorption does one experience the tranquil and sublime bliss;
therefore, the three consciousnesses are absent. Although the mental state of *vicāra* exists, it is so subtle that it does not manifest. In the fourth dhyāna, bliss is relinquished."

In the state of *saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is extinguished; because there is entirely no mind associated with *vicāra* (investigation), only the seven consciousnesses take the eighth consciousness as their object and constitute the nature of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

This is because they truly carry the objective essence (*sanimittālambana*), as they take a mind as their object and because the aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*) acts as an image (*pratibimba*) to serve as the object.

However, in the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because the seven consciousnesses have been extinguished, the aspect of seeing lacks a true carrying of the essence (*asanimittālambana*). Because...
Because there are no internal or external objects, it is called the "ear of the four empty heavens. Only the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* and five mental associates (*caitta*) remain;

however, upon reaching the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), these five mental associates cease to exist. This is because those who enter this meditative absorption have brought the mind to rest.
There remains only the seed of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), as the nature of the *anivṛtāvyākṛta-avidyā-vijñāna* has not yet been destroyed. Therefore, when the retribution is exhausted—
One returns to the cycle of saṃsāra. If one can sever the seeds of the self, one immediately abandons birth and death and becomes an arhat;
this is it. [The universal, specific, and wholesome mental factors are] eleven.
The treatise asks: Regarding the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), with which of the eight consciousnesses are they associated?

Furthermore, why are the object-specific mental factors (*viniyata*) not identical to the five universal mental factors? Moreover, with which consciousnesses are the eleven wholesome mental factors (*kuśala*) associated?
The answer states: As for the five universal mental factors, they are called "universal" because they pervade and function throughout all [consciousnesses].
The ground, all natures, and all minds, because they circulate and come and go without rest at all times;
furthermore, like ripples on water and like the nature of a torrential stream, they are called the "manifesting consciousness" (*ādarśa-vijñāna*) due to their nature of continuous flow.

These consist of the five mental factors—contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition—because both the internal and external must respond accordingly, even up to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Because they are still associated with the celestial realms, they are constant and uninterrupted; thus, they are called "universal" (*sarvatraga*). There are four meanings that constitute their universality.
As for these four meanings: first, they pervade all stages, up to the celestial realm of the fourth *ārūpya* heaven.
Because it is constantly associated [with them], it is said to pervade all stages (*bhūmi*); this can be understood regarding the lower realms. Second, it pervades all natures (*prakṛti*).

When seeds of good or evil encounter their objects, they are constantly associated with the five mental factors (*caitasika*)—attention (*manasikāra*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—and so forth;
thus, the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-prakṛti*) and others may likewise be understood. Therefore, there is no [distinction between] good and evil...

Third, it is called "pervasive of all natures" because it is applicable to all three natures. Fourth, it is called "pervasive of all minds," referring to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings;

because they correspond internally and externally—just as previously mentioned, through mental attention (*manasikāra*) and contact with objects—they give rise to all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states of mind.
Fifth, it is called "pervasive of all times," just like water.
The "floods" (ogha) are so named because they flow without interruption at all times; thus, they are said to pervade every moment. For these four reasons, they are called "universal" (sarvatraga).
As for the present mention of the "five mental factors" (caitta), it means that while the mind-king (citta-rāja) acts as the employer, the mental factors act as the employed.
Just as a father employs his son without opposition, they are therefore called "mental factors. Furthermore, there are forty others...
The six mental factors (*caitasika*) are also of this same meaning. Question: The meaning of the five mental factors is already known now;
however, as for the individual natures (*svabhāva*) and the individual functions and activities (*karma-vṛtti*) of these five mental factors, what is their meaning? Answer:

As for "nature," it refers to the specific seed-nature (*gotra*) of each [factor], which cannot be altered. As for the power of their activity, each possesses its own capacity. The remaining mental factors are also...
The general principles and meanings are already understood; now, each shall be analyzed individually and briefly explained through commentary.

△ Question: What is meant by the mental factor (*caitta*) called contact (*sparśa*)? Answer: That which is called contact refers to the conjunction of the sense faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

It is so named because it apprehends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon without yet being associated with names or linguistic designations (*nāma-pada*). Furthermore, contact is that which causes the mind—

Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the mental factors that contact their objects, and because it performs the specific function (*svakarma*) of feeling, perception, volition, and so forth, it is called "contact" (*sparśa*).

Just as with the contact of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna-sparśa*), the same applies to the contacts of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses; thus, they constitute the five types of contact.
Question: What is meant by the mental factor of *manasikāra* (attention)? Answer:

That which is called *manasikāra* refers to that which can alert the various mental factors—such as sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—by taking them as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is so named because it initiates the various mental factors and so forth as its own function (*karma*).
It is like being in a single room where, when one person first awakens, they startle and awaken all those in the room.
Therefore, because attention (*manasikāra*) is the most powerful among the other mental factors (*caitta*), it is so designated.
What is meant by "feeling" (*vedanā*)? The answer is: that which is called feeling refers to the experiencing of contact and so forth.

Because attention gives rise to the mind, one experiences objects that are either favorable or unfavorable. "Favorable" refers to pleasant objects; "unfavorable" means contrary, which refers to painful objects. This is because...

Feeling (*vedanā*) is so named because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the experiencing of objects that are either agreeable or disagreeable, and its function (*karman*) is the arising of minds such as aversion and attachment.

Furthermore, when objects are neither agreeable nor disagreeable, its intrinsic nature is the feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), and its function is the non-arising of minds such as aversion and attachment; thus it is called "feeling."

What is meant by "conceptualization" (*saṃjñā*)? The answer is: conceptualization is so called because it takes as its essential nature the grasping of images and the focused application [of attention] toward an object previously apprehended by the mental factor of sensation (*vedanā*).

Furthermore, it applies verbal designations to that apprehended object, such as whether it exists or does not exist, whether it is wholesome or unwholesome, or whether it is suffering or pleasure—thus giving rise to various names.
The various verbal expressions, being for the sake of one's own karma, are termed "perception" (*saṃjñā*); they have the mind’s discursive investigation (*vitarka*) as their essence.
What is meant by "volition" (*cetanā*)? Answer: That which is called volition refers to the mental factor of perception that aspires toward an object;
because it is not yet fixed, it further and more subtly examines the object of perception, and is thus termed "volition. It causes other states of mind...

Because it functions as a mental factor (*caitta*) that establishes objects of perception (*ālambana*) as being wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, its essential nature consists of the mental factor of investigation (*vicāra*).

As for the aforementioned perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), vitarka (*vitarka*), and vicāra, these are treated as independent factors in the state of distraction and will be analyzed later in the text.

However, when they occur within the Eightfold Noble Path, they constitute Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and Right Thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*); because they clearly comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they pervade the noble mind (*ārya-citta*).

Furthermore, the Tathāgata contemplated this matter for three weeks, fearing that if he were to preach the Supreme Vehicle first, sentient beings would not believe it and would instead incur downfall.

Therefore, he thought only of "name" (nāman). This concludes the explanation of the five omnipresent mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), including their respective natures and the power of their functions.

△ Next, the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca-viṣaya-niyata*) are explained: namely, desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), concentration (*samādhi*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

These are the five object-specific factors. △ Question: In what sense are they "object-specific"? Answer: Because their nature and function differ from those of the five previously mentioned universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitasika*).

Just as with the five previously mentioned mental factors (*caitta*), because of contact (*sparśa*) and the others, there arise attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) directed toward an object.
Therefore, because they are able to pervade all minds—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—they are [considered universal].

As for these "object-specific" (*viśeṣālambana*) factors, they arise in relation to distinct objects and do not extend to other objects; thus, they are termed "object-specific. Question: What is this?

Regarding the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*), do they each have their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or their function (*karman*)? Answer: Each shall be demonstrated individually. What is called "desire" (*chanda*)? Answer:
Desire refers to having the nature of aspiration toward objects of focus, such as the wholesome and so forth.

Its function is that even regarding unwholesome objects, it likewise relies upon the mind and diligence; it does not alter [the object], and for one who possesses desire, through craving, one immediately experiences [it]. It is not...

As for desire (*chanda*), because it is abandoned [in certain states], it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*); rather, it is subsumed under the category of object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).

What, then, is called resolve (*adhimokṣa*)? Answer: Resolve is so called because it maintains a firm conviction (*niścita-viṣaya*) regarding a determined object without error, and thus does not change;
this is its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Alternatively, it is the maintenance of a firm conviction within the objects of words and meanings, being entirely free from error.

Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is that which cannot be deluded or confused by others; because its specific function (*karma*) is to turn [the mind] toward other objects without being diverted;
and because if one is hesitant, it does not constitute the distinct object of "resolute belief" (*adhimokṣa*), whereas if one is not hesitant, it is therefore called a "distinct object.
As for why it is not a "universal factor" (*sarvatraga*) but is instead subsumed under the "distinct objects": it is because it follows after various states of mind. How, then, is it named?

Question: What is meant by "mindfulness" (*smṛti*)? Answer: That which is called mindfulness has as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) the causing of the mind to clearly remember and not forget an object previously experienced.
Its specific function (*karma*) is to rely upon an object previously experienced without abandoning it. If it takes up another object, it does not constitute mindfulness;
therefore, it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), but is subsumed under the category of object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
What is meant by "wisdom" (prajñā)? The answer is: that which is called "contemplating the object" has the nature of discernment and decisive resolution with clarity;
it has the function of severing doubt and establishing firm conviction.

Alternatively, although the false views of non-Buddhists do not err regarding their objects, because they cling to the five aggregates and so forth through the two views of eternalism and nihilism, these are subsumed under "false wisdom" and are not right view.

Furthermore, since wisdom (*prajñā*) makes a definitive determination without error and does not shift toward other factors, it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), but is instead subsumed under the "object-specific" (*viṣayapratiniyata*) category.

Question: In which consciousnesses is it included? Answer: Although the verse and commentary state that these object-specific factors exist within the five sensory consciousnesses, their inclusion within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is likewise not outside the scope of possibility.
Why is this? Because the objects of desire can be common to the five consciousnesses; thus, they pertain to all six consciousnesses.

Within this, one achieves resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). Although it may sometimes be clear through a single instance of seeing, or even within the five sensory consciousnesses, it is nonetheless achieved within the sixth consciousness.

Why is this? For how could one who lacks definitive volition (*cetanā*) be able to establish a seal of certainty? If mindfulness were not sustained by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), [it would be impossible].
How can meditative concentration (*samādhi*) be established? If there were no mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), how could one focus the mind on a single object?

If wisdom (*prajñā*) lacked the mind, it would be unable to deliberate and discern; thus, the treatise on wisdom would not be established. Furthermore, [wisdom] also extends to the seven [sensory] consciousnesses, for they constitute false wisdom.
I do not dare to be dogmatic in this matter; I request that those of lofty wisdom investigate it, remaining unconstrained by any fixed position. Next, the eleventh [topic] is discussed.
This is also one of the wholesome mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*).
△ Question: The Buddha possesses immeasurable great virtues; how could these be accomplished by only eleven mental factors?
Answer: This shall be distinguished in the subsequent text. Now, "wholesome" (*śubha*) means "beautiful. Thus, Laozi said: "Venerable words may be..."

It is acquired through exchange; it may also be acquired by means of a person through preparatory effort (*prayoga*). If one does not calculate its merit, it constitutes supramundane goodness (*lokottara-kuśala*).

Combining these types of goodness, they are said to be both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), because they result in pure and sublime fruits. Question: Among the eleven factors of wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*), [which...]
How do these eleven wholesome factors pertain to the five sensory consciousnesses? Furthermore, how is it that each possesses its own intrinsic nature and its own functional activity?

Answer: Regarding the eleven wholesome factors: first, faith; second, shame (*hrī*); third, dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); fourth, non-attachment (*alobha*); fifth, non-hatred (*adveṣa*); sixth, non-delusion (*amoha*). Question:
Do these six wholesome mental factors pertain to the five sensory consciousnesses? Answer: They do, by virtue of the seeds of wholesome states previously perfumed in the past.
Therefore, through seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, and touching with the body, one gives rise to faith in the Three Jewels.

Consequently, one realizes that the transgressions previously committed were not due to having seen the virtues of the noble ones; thus, shame and remorse arise spontaneously without being taught, leading to confession.
Because of the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion in the past, when encountering objects through sight, hearing, or touch, there is no greed, no hatred, and no delusion.
It is so. If there are seeds of greed and other afflictions, then there is simply no nature of liberation.

Furthermore, as for the five wholesome mental factors (*caitasika*), they are definitely associated with the five consciousnesses in the same way, and they also extend to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Why is this? If one exerts diligent effort, there are two aspects:
first, because the body does not quickly become weary, it belongs to the body-consciousness; second, because the mind does not grow fatigued, it encompasses the mental consciousness.
If both body and mind are neither weary nor lax, it is called diligence (*vīrya*). Regarding heedfulness (*apramāda*), there are also two types:
first, bodily heedfulness, such as [the restraint of] the body and speech, because they pertain to the body-consciousness; second, mental heedfulness, because it pertains to the mental consciousness.

As for the tenth practice, equanimity (*upekṣā*): it is directed toward the practice of equanimity; encountering objects, one relinquishes them spontaneously, acting without being taught, and thus accomplishing it naturally.
These also belong to the eye and ear, as well as to seeing, hearing, mental formation, and equanimity; they also pertain to the mind. The eleventh is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Because it was previously cultivated through a compassionate mind that benefits others, when one encounters an object, compassion arises, which is precisely non-harming.

Regarding these eleven virtuous mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), the ancients said they belong to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*). This is explained from the perspective of the majority of cases. However, according to my own analysis, this is also...
Furthermore, the mental consciousness lacks a fixed standard. Question: What is the meaning of "each according to its own nature" and "each according to its own karma"?
Answer: Each shall be demonstrated individually.
Question: What is meant by faith (*śraddhā*)? Answer: Faith is the mind’s clarity characterized by profound acceptance, delight, and aspiration toward reality and virtue;
it takes this as its intrinsic nature. Its function is to counteract lack of faith and to sever doubt.
Therefore, lack of faith is the root obstacle to the Noble Path, whereas faith is the source and origin of the Eightfold Noble Path. Furthermore, there are three ways in which doubt arises. First:
Devas, humans, non-Buddhists, seers, and others cling to the aggregates characterized by the four marks, such as "self" and "person.

If they hear the profound Dharma, they immediately give rise to doubt and slander. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Because they destroy the Dharma and do not believe in it, they fall into the three evil realms.
By the power of their lack of faith, they obstruct the Path. Second, the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna and the Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles do not...
Because those who believe in the Mahāyāna lack the power to enter the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom. Third, when Bodhisattvas do not have faith, it is not that they lack faith;
rather, they possess a web of doubt. This is like how one in the stage of "seeing the path" (darśana-mārga) cannot enter the stage of "cultivating the path" (bhāvanā-mārga) due to a web of doubt;

or how a Bodhisattva in the stage of cultivating the path cannot enter the stage of realizing the path (sākṣātkriyā-mārga) due to a web of doubt; or how those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) do not see the Tathāgata.

That which is a supreme and wondrous object becomes a net of doubt. Because one must apply the power of diligence with particular intensity, only then can the net of doubt be severed and the eight dharma-realms be attained.
Thus it is said: "Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit. And again:
"Faith enables one to surely reach the stage of the Tathāgata. This is faith. Question: Among all forms of goodness, why is faith considered the foremost? Answer:
Did we not say previously? "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit. It is by the power of faith that one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
Therefore, when Sudhana reached the presence of the Great Being Maitreya, he still took the power of faith and the bodhicitta as his primary focus before entering the Samantabhadra Bodhimanda.
Thus, faith is like the "dust-settling jewel" (śānta-rajas-maṇi) that can settle all dust to its very end.

Regarding the various objects (*dharmas*): because they do not obstruct the path to liberation, they are like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), for there is nothing that cannot be obtained according to one's heart's desire;
and they are like a sharp sword, for they completely pierce through all afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, among the eleven wholesome factors, faith is made the foremost.
Second is *hrī* (shame). What is meant by *hrī*? The answer is: *hrī* means shame.
It refers to looking within oneself and recognizing that all past transgressions and faults were committed out of ignorance; now that one has realized this, shame arises. It is shame.

Therefore, for a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), the two states of mind—shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)—serve as adornments. Thus, the character for "shame" (*hrī*) signifies the reception of what is wholesome.

It is the foremost of all [virtues]. It initiates wholesome dharmas. The *Śāstra* states: "Taking the power of the Dharma as its basis, honoring and revering the noble and holy ones is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
bringing to rest unwholesome conduct is its function (*karma*). For example, there was a certain stainless bhikṣu who violated the precept against sexual misconduct.
Whenever he sees any śrāmaṇeras who maintain the precepts, he bows down to them all, saying: "I have violated the precept against sexual misconduct;
I shall surely fall into hell. I beg the assembly of monks to grant me repentance for my transgression. *Cān* means shame; it is the cessation of evil conduct.

The third is shame (*hrī*). What is meant by shame? The answer is: as for that which is called shame, whenever one has committed a transgression oneself, upon seeing any noble being, parent, teacher, or elder, one becomes filled with shame.
It is like a person who, having drunk wine and become greatly intoxicated, falls into a foul-smelling mire;
once he has sobered up, none of his kinsmen can recognize him. When one sees such external [conditions]...
Human beings are all equally possessed of a sense of shame; this is what is meant by "shame" (*hrī*). Thus, the treatise states:
"Shame has as its intrinsic nature the rejection of various evils through the power of worldly wholesome forces.

For example, just as one feels shame when another commits an evil, so too does one feel shame regarding one's own transgressions. Furthermore, in contrast to "lack of shame," it is defined as the cessation of unwholesome conduct.
Because of karma, those among humans who possess a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are able to sever evil, cultivate goodness, and achieve sainthood;
even those who transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*) instantaneously, severing hindrances and realizing the truth, all attain such accomplishment through shame and dread of blame.
Therefore it is said: "If a person lacks a sense of shame and remorse, all evils will be accomplished; this is the foremost of transgressions.

How much more so when one has committed an offense—how could one fail to repent? For this reason, those who have not yet attained the Way, upon seeing one who has realized the Way, give rise to shame and remorse.
Those who have already seen the Way, if they see one who cultivates the Way and possesses virtue, further give rise to shame and remorse.

Furthermore, when a practitioner on the path of cultivation encounters one who has realized the path of seeing, they must give rise to even greater shame and remorse before they can attain realization.
Even within the fruits of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), if one beholds the stage of the Tathāgata’s fruition, one cannot realize it without being struck with profound shame and remorse.
Thus, shame and remorse extend all the way to the ranks of the sages; how much more so for those like us within the triple world (*tridhātu*)—how could we not give rise to shame?
How truly lamentable! Regarding the four types of non-attachment (*alobha*):
what is meant by "non-attachment"? The answer is: that which is called non-attachment refers to [freedom from craving for] the first, external wealth;
the second, internal wealth; the third, one's retinue; the fourth, fame; the fifth, profit; the sixth, sleep; the seventh, sexual desire; the eighth, food and drink; and the ninth, clothing.
10. Each [of these] is a dust-like beautiful object; 11. Mind, thought, and consciousness—those above all belong to ordinary worldly sentiments. 12.
The vision of the sages is entirely subsumed within non-attachment. However, if there is even a single instance of not relinquishing [them], one does not become a Great Sage.
Furthermore, the first ten types of relinquishment involve external forms (*rūpa*), while the latter one type involves mental factors (*citta-dharma*).
Moreover, the first ten types relinquish external objects, whereas the latter two types relinquish internal objects.

That which is not relinquished is comprised of the affliction of self-love (*ātma-sneha*) and the seeds of the innate self and phenomena (*sahaja-ātmadharma-bīja*). That which is relinquished is termed non-attachment (*alobha*).

Question: Since it has already been stated that non-attachment (*alobha*) is synonymous with relinquishment (*tyāga*), why must "relinquishing equanimity" (*upekṣā-saṃskāra*) be established separately later on?

Answer: Non-attachment belongs to the mind, whereas relinquishing equanimity belongs to the object. It is only by virtue of the internal mind being free from attachment that one is able to practice relinquishing equanimity.

If there were attachment within, how could one possibly practice relinquishing equanimity? As the treatise says: "One who is without attachment is without clinging toward existence (*bhava*) and the requisites of existence (*bhava-pariṣkāra*). This is for oneself...
Because its nature is such that it acts as an antidote to greed by performing wholesome deeds, and because it seeks to bring about the tainted fruits of the three realms, it is called "non-greed.
This fully encompasses the meanings mentioned previously.

Fifth is non-anger (*adveṣa*). What is meant by non-anger? The answer is: regarding non-anger, it means that what accords with my mind I necessarily crave, while what opposes my mind I necessarily resent.
For example, if one takes away what I love—be it wealth, a wife, children, or kinsmen—I will certainly give rise to anger.
If I were without craving, then even if such things were taken away, anger would certainly not arise. Therefore, it is called non-anger.

Just as the elephant’s mate did not give rise to thoughts of retaliation when harmed by a hunter, she was thus without anger. Even when encountering the most extreme instruments of suffering, her patience remained sufficient because of these four conditions;
this is non-anger (*adveṣa*). Therefore, the treatise states that non-anger has the nature of being free from malice toward suffering and the instruments of suffering.
It serves as the antidote to anger, ensuring it does not arise, and instead takes the cultivation of wholesome thoughts and diligence as its essence.
Because of karma, or if one encounters an evil person who seizes one's robes and bowl, one does not give rise to thoughts of anger;

instead, one arouses a mind of loving-kindness—this is non-hatred. Sixth is non-delusion. What is non-delusion? Answer: Non-delusion means that when encountering objects and circumstances, one is resolute.
One is not deluded. Because one knows that these objects are illusory and fundamentally empty, one remains resolutely undeluded throughout the twelve periods of the day and night;
thus, there is no ignorance. As the *Śāstra* states: "Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is clear understanding regarding phenomena and principles.

Its primary function is to counteract the grasping at delusive objects and, conversely, to perform virtuous deeds as its own activity. This "clear understanding" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Because the object is definitively non-erroneous, one clearly understands the principle and comprehends the phenomenon; thus, one does not err regarding the principle of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
For this reason, it is designated by the name "non-delusion" (amoha).
Seventh is diligent vigor (vīrya). What is called "diligence" (kō), and what are called "purity" (se) and "advancement" (shin)? Answer: As for diligence—

It continues without ceasing day and night. The *Śāstra* states: "Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is vigor (*vīrya*) regarding the matters of cultivating the wholesome and abandoning the unwholesome;
and because its function (*karma*) is to counteract laziness and fulfill the wholesome. The commentary explains: "The wholesome is to be cultivated and the unwholesome is to be abandoned.
'Vigor' means not shrinking from toil and hardship; this refers to the Dharma of the Four Right Efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*)."
This is what is included therein: namely, causing that which has already been abandoned to never arise again; applying effort to abandon those unwholesome states not yet abandoned;
preserving and not losing those wholesome states already cultivated; and resolutely cultivating those wholesome states not yet cultivated.
Therefore, one who lacks a courageous mind can certainly not progress. Because it is able to abandon [the unwholesome], it is called "vigor" (*vīrya*) and is indeed "diligence" (*pragata*).

Eighth is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). What is meant by "pliancy"? Because one applies oneself to the cultivation of the path with diligence and vigor, free from the aforementioned hindrances of greed, hatred, and delusion, one attains that which is light and peaceful.
That which is called "light" refers to the relinquishing of heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*);

that which is called "peaceful" refers to the attainment of mental tranquility and the realization of the fundamental source. As the treatise states: "By means of distancing oneself from heaviness and rigidity..."
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the pliancy of body and mind that renders them capable of bearing [the task].

Its primary function (*karmasvaka*) is to counteract lethargy (*styāna*) and to bring about the purity of the fundamental transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). As for *praśrabdhi* (serenity/pliancy), it is the initial stage of practice.
If one proceeds to the subsequent stage, then through the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*), the essence becomes perfected; this is the fruit of serenity.

The ninth is non-negligence (*apramāda*). What is meant by "non-negligence"? The answer is: The ancient masters said, "Guard the mouth as one would a sealed jar; guard the mind as one would a city. Thus:
when opening the mouth and moving the tongue, do not open it if there is no benefit to others;

when lifting the feet and taking steps, do not lift them if there is no benefit to others; when raising the mind and stirring thoughts, do not stir them if there is no benefit to others. Therefore, [these are the five...].
The *Śāstra* (Treatise) states: "That which is called 'firmness' is so named because one does not abandon the practice of the precepts; it is precisely what is termed 'heedfulness' (*apramāda*).

The *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* states: Because its intrinsic nature consists of the constant protection [of the mind] through every thought-moment—whether in cultivation or abandonment—by means of the three roots of previous diligence, namely non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
and because it serves to bring to fulfillment all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds."
Because it is one's own karma, it is also another name for diligence; therefore, it is called non-negligence (*apramāda*).

If one examines this closely, it severs the seeds of self-love and leads to the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, as well as the stage of the fruit of Tathāgata-hood—all through the power of diligence.
How could one not believe this?

The ten types of equanimity (*upekṣā*). What is meant by "equanimity in practice"? The answer is: regarding internal and external wealth and so forth, one relinquishes them all without stinginess, even including one's kin;
one likewise abandons them. Furthermore, toward both enemies and friends, one brings them all to liberation and does not dwell upon past transgressions;
this is what is called "equanimity in practice. The treatise states: "Equanimity" means, through the three faculties of diligence, causing the mind...
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) never arises; its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is straightforwardness and effortlessness (*anābhoga*).

Its primary function (*karma*) is to counteract restlessness (*auddhatya*) and to cause the mind to abide in tranquility. Furthermore, there are three types of equanimity: first, the equanimity that abandons ordinary worldly sentiments.
First, it is because [this] constitutes the seeds of all afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion. Second, it is because one abandons the noble vision (*āryadṛṣṭi*);

for example, just as those of the Two Vehicles cling to *nirvāṇa*, and because one cannot escape [bondage] through the wisdom of signless contemplation (*animittabhāvanā*) applied during the seventh stage.

Now, if one were to abandon this, one would be abandoning the seeds of the noble vision. Third, it is because one abandons the characteristic of wisdom (*jñānalakṣaṇa*). Within the section on the Buddha’s path of realization (*bodhimārga*), by means of...
The characteristics of wisdom are eternally stilled; therefore, it is said that "perfecting bodhi returns to non-attainment," which is precisely what is called relinquishment (*tyāga*).
This is because, by means of relinquishment, one abandons the final seeds of deluded nature and is liberated from the final seeds of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
For this reason, the single character "relinquishment" extends throughout the stage of Buddhahood.
Eleventh is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). What is meant by non-harming? The answer is:

non-harming is, for example, when King Kali was dismembered limb by limb yet still did not give rise to anger; instead, he maintained a primary state of compassion. It is also like a hunter who wounded an elephant.
Because one perceives that those stained by passion do not give rise to anger toward others as a whole and thus do not inflict harm, the treatise states:
"One does not cause injury or affliction to sentient beings, because non-anger is its intrinsic nature; it is able to counteract the intent to harm."

On the contrary, because making compassionate concern for sentient beings one’s own primary activity, the Tathāgata reflected during the three weeks [following his enlightenment] that he did not dare preach the Mahāyāna, fearing it might harm the roots of goodness in sentient beings; thus it is said he does no harm.
For example, when a mosquito or gnat bites a person who possesses the seed of compassion, they immediately protect its life with their hand and remove it; thus it is said they do no harm.
Regarding these eleven types of wholesome dharmas, is there a sequential order? Answer: Yes, there is a sequence.
First, by the power of deep faith, one certainly gives rise to shame for the evil previously committed; from this, the mind of *hrī* (moral dread) arises.
Therefore, whenever one encounters the objects of the five sensory realms, one naturally does not covet them.
This is because one already knows that by coveting wealth, beauty, fame, and profit, one creates various transgressions; thus, one relinquishes them and does not crave them.

Because one does not crave these sensory objects, even if someone harms me or robs me of my possessions, I do not feel anger. Why is it that I do not feel anger? It is because I have attained awakening.

Regarding the preceding objects: because the illusory realm is empty, one is not deluded. Due to the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion, one seeks exclusively the supramundane path and applies oneself with diligent vigor.
By the power of this vigor, one attains physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

One attains the sublime benefit of the Dharma. By the power of having attained this sublime benefit, fearing the loss of the noble wealth, one’s three karmas of body, speech, and mind become, moment by moment, free from negligence.
Because of this non-negligence, one perceives, moment by moment, that which is within the triple world.
Because there is nothing to be cherished, one practices equanimity (*upekṣā*) at all times.

By practicing equanimity, as in the case of King Kali who, even when his body was being dismembered, gave rise to no thought of anger but instead conceived a mind of compassionate rescue; thus, he did not cause harm. This is precisely the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Furthermore, the first ten mental states are cultivated by those of the three vehicles, while the final single mind of non-harming is transformed into great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which is universal.
The Mahāyāna and the Supreme Vehicle are simply the stage of the Tathāgata.
However, within the Hīnayāna, one gives rise to shame and remorse through the power of faith, such that desire never arises again;

only by eventually attaining the mind of equanimity does one escape birth and death. Within the Mahāyāna, by first relying on the power of faith, one suddenly shatters the realm of ignorance and delusion.
Realizing that objects are fundamentally empty, one does not give rise to greed or anger, but proceeds even unto equanimity (*upekṣā*), never causing harm.

Seeing sentient beings undergo suffering, one instead gives rise to thoughts of compassion and rescues them. While the Hīnayāna is solely for self-benefit, the Mahāyāna fully possesses both benefits for self and others;
thus, the eleven mental states are accomplished. Furthermore, non-greed constitutes the practice of equanimity and fulfills generosity (*dāna*).
Because one transcends greed through giving, shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and heedfulness (*apramāda*) constitute the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
By the power of maintaining ethical discipline, one transcends heedlessness, as a sense of shame arises in every moment of thought.

Non-anger (*avyāpāda*) and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) constitute the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*); by the power of forbearance, one transcends anger and the intent to harm sentient beings. Diligence (*vīrya*) is...
Vigor is endowed with [the perfection of] vigor because it delivers the heedless mind; serenity is endowed with the perfection of meditation because it delivers through meditative absorption;
and non-delusion is the perfection of wisdom, for it delivers delusion by means of the sublime wisdom of *prajñā*.
Furthermore, because one does not harbor anger, one instead practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*); because one does not cause harm, one gives rise to compassion (*karuṇā*).
Moreover, from the absence of anger, joy (*muditā*) arises, and one practices equanimity (*upekṣā*), whereby enemies and kin are regarded as equal; thus it is called "equanimity.

Therefore, these eleven wholesome mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) extensively pervade the three vehicles (*yāna*), the four fruits of the path, and all dharmas such as the perfections (*pāramitā*) and the myriad practices. This extends even to the third...
The seventeen categories of factors that aid the path (*saptadaśa-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are likewise all applicable; this can be understood by reflecting upon them.
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* concerning the "two middling and eight great [afflictions] of greed, anger, and delusion":
this single phrase should not be explained according to the sequence of the literal text, but rather interpreted according to the sequence of its meaning; only then can it follow.
First, there are six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). Second, there are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), divided into three categories:
first, eight major secondary afflictions; second, two medium secondary afflictions; and third, ten minor secondary afflictions, totaling twenty.
When these are added to the six root afflictions, they constitute twenty-six afflictions; these are the afflictions of ordinary sentient beings.
These are mental factors (*caitta*), which are non-noble dharmas (*anāryadharma*). They are abandoned at the stage of the eighth ground Bodhisattva.

Regarding the six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) mentioned in the section on the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), it simply states "three roots," namely the three afflictions of greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).
Furthermore, the "three roots" also refers to the three types of affliction consisting of pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
In the chapter on the seven consciousnesses, the three fundamental [afflictions] are explained:
first, greed; second, hatred; and third, delusion. As for what is called greed, it consists of coveting the property of others.
Applying this to oneself: regarding the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), as well as wealth, sensual pleasure, fame, food, clothing, and so forth, greed arises simultaneously with them.
Therefore, the treatise states: "To have a nature that gives rise to defiled attachment toward both existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence (*bhava-pariṣkāra*);

it can obstruct non-greed (*alobha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*); and its function is to produce suffering. For example, when the Buddha was formerly a king, due to his greed for wealth and sensual pleasure, he caused harm...
One falls into the three evil realms and subsequently becomes a jackal. Only by relying on the power of wisdom can one be born within the Tuṣita heaven in the presence of the Sage;
thus, the single word "greed" is the root of all suffering. Regarding the second [precept], "restrain and be cautious":
as for "hatred," if others act against me, I immediately give rise to resentment and anger toward my own wealth, wife, children, and so forth.
"Kuan": When one's gains of fame and profit are seized or schemed away by others, one immediately gives rise to resentment; this is what is meant by "hatred" (*dveṣa*). The *Śāstra* states:
"To increase hatred toward the most painful conditions is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Its primary function (*karma*) is to obstruct non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and cause the mind to be unsettled.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "In a single thought-moment, when a heart of hatred arises, eighty thousand gates of obstruction open. Yama... [text ends]
King Lohita was once the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, yet when his military forces were inferior [to those of the Buddha], he gave rise to a single thought of anger.

Consequently, in future lives, he became the Lord of Hell to govern people such as yourselves. Thus, every day, he brings upon himself the ordeal of having molten copper poured into his mouth three times;
all this is the result of thoughts of anger. How painful! How bitter! Be most earnestly cautioned against it.
Third is delusion (*moha*). What is delusion? It is to be confused regarding all objective spheres (*viṣaya*), being bewildered by illusory appearances.

Because one does not clearly understand phenomena and principles, one interprets them erroneously; thus, within all objects, a mind of grasping arises. Therefore, it is called delusion. The treatise states:
"Its intrinsic nature is confusion and bewilderment regarding all phenomena and principles. It functions as an obstacle to non-deluded, pure wisdom (*vimala-prajñā*).
It is karma. For example, Devadatta sought to harm the Buddha, and King Ajātaśatru killed his father to become a new king;
how could they have become new Buddhas? Therefore, it is due to delusion.
The three types of afflictions mentioned above are associated with the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*). Why is this?

Because when the five consciousnesses perceive the objects of the five sensory realms, that which is favorable to the self gives rise to greed; that which is unfavorable to the self gives rise to anger; and the failure to discern the facts and principles constitutes delusion.

At the moment the five consciousnesses come into contact with the objects of the five sensory realms, they immediately draw forth the seeds of greed and anger, which have been pre-established. If one falls into the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), [the process continues further].

Inference (*anumāna*): Furthermore, the accumulation of karma occurs now within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) as they take objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as their domain. These are immediately associated with craving and other afflictions.
This can be understood through the example of a child less than one year old: although lacking cognitive awareness, the child feels attachment upon seeing money and feels anger when it is taken away.
Thus, it is evident that [the mind] is associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as with the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*), the seeds of self-love (*ātma-sneha-bīja*), and so forth.
It is associated with the four afflictions. Why is this? Because there is the seed of the thief within and the objects of craving without, they only then come into association.
Therefore, although this is discussed in relation to the five consciousnesses, it is actually induced by the seeds and so forth of the eighth consciousness; this is the natural principle.
It is only when the emotions of the seventh consciousness arise that they rely upon the six consciousnesses to manifest as good or evil. [This refers to] the seeds of the various afflictions.
The [secondary] afflictions (*upakleśa*) are also treated according to this same principle. Question: What constitutes the "root" [afflictions]? Answer:

Because the three types of afflictions—the minor (*parīttakleśabhūmika*), the secondary (*upakleśabhūmika*), and the major (*mahābhūmika*)—all arise based upon these six root [afflictions], they are therefore called "root afflictions.

For example, among the minor secondary afflictions, there are those such as anger (*krodha*) and resentment (*upanāha*), as well as flattery (*māyā*) and deception (*śāṭhya*). This is because the mental factor of anger...
Enmity and its like depend on the root of hatred; flattery, deception, and so forth depend on the root of greed;

lack of shame, lack of remorse, and the eight secondary mental factors (upakleśas) depend on the root of delusion. Other mental factors may be understood by analogy with these cases; therefore, they are called "roots."
Furthermore, these seeds of greed, hatred, and delusion pervade the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and, until the end of the future, they harm the life-force of the *dharmakāya*;

thus, they are termed the "roots of the three poisons. Regarding the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are twenty mental factors (*caitta*) that arise entirely in dependence upon the root afflictions;
they are called "secondary" (*anu*) because they follow after the roots. Furthermore, they are divided into three categories.
Classification: First, the Major Derivatives; Second, the Intermediate Derivatives; Third, the Minor Derivatives. What are the Major Derivatives? The answer is:
they are called "Major" because they possess three characteristics. They are called "Derivatives" because they take delusion and doubt as their fundamental basis.
Next, what are the three characteristics? First, they arise within their own category; for example, when a state of lack of faith arises, then indolence and negligence [also arise].

This is because states such as negligence (pramāda) arise gradually. Second, they possess a pervasive defiled nature, which means they are of the nature of unwholesomeness (akuśala) or neutrality (avyākṛta).

Third, they pervade defiled minds, meaning they extend through both internal and external consciousnesses. Possessing these three characteristics, they are termed "great universal" (mahābhūmika) afflictions.
Regarding the two medium [unwholesome mental factors], they arise only from their own kind (*sva-jātīya*) in a single sense. What is meant by "arising from their own kind in a single sense"?

It means that when the mind of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) arises, it arises spontaneously as a homogeneous type together with the mind of lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). Therefore, they are called "medium.

Because they follow along with delusion (*moha*), which is their root, they are specifically termed "medium secondary" (*anuśaya*). Regarding the three minor [unwholesome mental factors], because they lack these three meanings, they are all [minor].
They are called "minor" because anger and its associates follow from the root of hatred, while stinginess and its associates depend upon the root of greed;

thus they are merely termed "minor associates. Furthermore, the minor associates correspond only with the sixth consciousness and possess an unwholesome nature, and do not correspond with other consciousnesses;
hence they are called "minor. Because they rely upon the three roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, they are so named.

Regarding the two types of *anuvartana* (conformity) within the category of *anuvartana*: logically, they should follow after the section on *anuvartana*. However, following the verse-text of the Great Master Xuanzang, they are discussed first.
First is *āhrīkya* (lack of shame). What is meant by "lack of shame"? It refers to when one possesses faults and transgressions, yet conversely regards them as being right.
Furthermore, one reverses oneself to disparage those who possess virtue, regarding their excellence as a fault; thus it is called "lack of shame" (*ahrī*).
It is like a person who opposes his elders yet considers himself capable; hence he is without shame. The *Śāstra* says:

"To disregard shame and take one's own nature as non-virtuous, and conversely to slight and reject the worthy and good because they are the very nature of others"—therefore, by obstructing the Noble Path with the dragon-like hindrance, the mind of shame increases.
Because one takes long-term evil conduct as one's own karma, it is called *āhrīkya* (lack of shame).
Second is *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread). What is meant by "lack of dread"? The answer is:

to commit evil while regarding it as non-faulty, and conversely, to appeal to others by claiming one's own talents as superior and asserting them as one's capability; therefore, it is called lack of dread. The treatise states: "It disregards the world."
There are those who possess virtue, yet they revere and honor the violent and evil, taking it as their own nature that the most powerful is supreme.
Furthermore, because it obstructs the noble path and causes the sense of shame (*hrī*) to increase in its capacity for unwholesome conduct, it is called "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*). Question:

How are the two mental states of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) distinguished? Answer: Lack of shame is the failure to fear others; it refers to speaking behind one's back.

No. "Lack of shame" (āhrīkya) is the opposite of exposing one's faults to others and having no fear of being rebuked face-to-face. Thus, because *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (dread of blame) differ in their coarseness and subtlety, they are divided into two.
Among the three great categories, there are eight [sub-factors]. Regarding the two factors of restlessness (*auddhatya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*): their characteristics are as follows.
Restlessness is like the mind of a bird or a magpie; it constantly delights in worldly objects as its pleasure and never earnestly seeks tranquility.
It obstructs the noble stages; because it has no connection whatsoever with any *samādhi*, it is called *auddhatya* (restlessness).
The treatise states: "Its nature is to cause the mind to be non-quiescent regarding its object; its function is to obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*) and *śamatha*.
Regarding *śamatha*: in this land [China], it is called "stopping" (*zhi*). Therefore, it is named "equanimity of practice" (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), for it relinquishes all views.
Second, regarding *styāna* (sloth): because one who is prone to agitation (*auddhatya*) does not seek tranquility, the spirit becomes weary and exhausted.

Consequently, whether hearing the Dharma or practicing seated meditation, a state of sloth arises in the mind. Thus, the treatise states that it renders the mind unserviceable with respect to the objects of the noble dharmas;
therefore, its function is to obstruct *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) and the practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight). *Vipaśyanā*...

Regarding the term "pātra" (bowl): in this region, it is called a "louguan" (viewing tower) because it signifies "observing. It is also said that while previously it obstructed *śamatha* (calm abiding), now it obstructs *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Because these two mental factors are present, they obstruct the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, such that one never enters the Path.
How truly painful and lamentable!
Regarding the three types of lack of faith: because of the two preceding mental factors, one is unable to enter the Path. It is as with Rāhula;
when he first left home to become a śrāmaṇera, he was fond of restlessness and did not understand the Dharma upon hearing it, and thus lacked faith and wished to return to secular life.
Later, the Buddha used skillful means to lead them toward faith; thus, they were able to attain the fruit. The *Śāstra* states:
"Its nature is a turbid mind that cannot accept, find pleasure in, or desire the reality of virtues and their bases. Furthermore, it can obstruct pure faith, taking indolence as its function.

Now, lack of faith is the foremost obstacle to the Path and the cause for slandering the Dharma; by this, one falls into the three evil realms. It is through this that [the state of non-belief] is established.

Furthermore, as for the fourth type, laziness: because one does not apply the mind with earnest intent toward the sublime Dharma, one does not cultivate respectful devotion toward the Triple Gem, and regarding spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one does not listen to the Dharma;
even if one does listen, one does not practice it diligently. Therefore, this is called laziness.

*kausīdya* (laziness). The treatise states: Its nature is indolence regarding the cultivation of wholesome qualities and the abandonment of unwholesome ones; its function is to obstruct diligence and increase defilement.
Within the context of cultivation and abandonment, it consists in not cultivating what is wholesome that ought to be cultivated, and not abandoning what is unwholesome that ought to be abandoned.
Consequently, the thought of diligence never enters [the mind]. It is itself a defiled mind of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because it causes [unwholesome states] to increase, it is called indolence (*kausīdya*).
As for the five forms of negligence (*pramāda*): they are like a horse without a tether or a bird without a cage; thus, one lets them loose and allows them to roam at will.
"Letting loose" means not restraining the mind; "roaming at will" means being wild. Because one acts according to one's own whims, it is called negligence. This is...
It is the root of breaking the precepts and the leader in the creation of karma; thus, for one who is negligent, it obstructs the goodness of diligence.
The *Śāstra* states: "Within the categories of the defiled and the pure, it is characterized by a lack of restraint and cultivation, having heedlessness as its nature.
Its function is to obstruct the goodness of non-heedlessness, increasing evil and diminishing good. 'Unable to restrain and cultivate' means being unable to guard and protect the body and speech."
Because one commits transgressions through the three karmas of the mind, one is unable to cultivate the observance of the precepts regarding the three karmas of body, speech, and mind;
therefore, this is called negligence (*pramāda*). Sixth, loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*): due to the aforementioned laziness and negligence, one loses right mindfulness and fails to...
It is exceedingly remote from the mundane and supramundane dharmas that can be entered. The *Śāstra* states: Its nature is the inability to clearly retain the object of focus;
its function is to obstruct right mindfulness in entering the Path and to serve as the basis for distraction.
Because one cannot clearly retain the Noble Path, the mind becomes distracted; this is called "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛtitā*).
Seven types of distraction. Question: What is the difference between agitation (*auddhatya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*)?

Answer: Agitation is the mind’s rushing toward external objects; distraction is the lack of tranquility within the internal mind. At one time it is directed toward wholesome thoughts, and at another toward unwholesome thoughts;

at one time there is faith, and at another lack of faith; at one time there is understanding, and at another lack of understanding; or else, one practices this [meditation] but does not achieve it. Furthermore...
