Thus, through the power of reflection (*cintā*), it may become wholesome, unwholesome, or neither; therefore, the mind of reflection is called "undetermined.
Hence, a book says: "It is well to reflect twice; only then does it become determined."
What is meant by "sleep"? It refers to when, while engaging in wholesome activities such as reciting scriptures or practicing seated meditation, one encounters physical fatigue;

thus, one first nourishes and rests so that one may subsequently perform wholesome deeds. Alternatively, if one encounters a wholesome object but succumbs to indolence and fails to follow along with various wholesome acts, this is termed "unwholesome.
Because these two states—wholesome and unwholesome—are not fixed, it is called the "indeterminate mind."
What is called "regret"? It refers to having previously performed a wholesome deed but later encountering an evil friend who slanders that goodness, thereby giving rise to regret;
or having previously committed an unwholesome act but later encountering a virtuous friend who rebukes it, thereby giving rise to regret. For this reason, it is called an indeterminate state of mind.
However, the two mental factors of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) pertain to all six consciousnesses, as well as the seventh consciousness;

they do not pertain to the eighth consciousness. Thus, the explanation in the treatise regarding how these aforementioned fourteen mental factors are subsumed under the manovijñāna (mental consciousness) is hereby concluded.
Question: Regarding the temporary assignment of good and evil to their respective realms, how is it that they are assigned at such a time? Answer:

As for what is called "assignment," it is because the seeds of good and evil, perfumed since beginningless time, are stored within the *ālayavijñāna* by the seven consciousnesses; therefore, [they manifest] now.
When one encounters a wholesome object, a wholesome manifestation arises; when one encounters an unwholesome object, an unwholesome manifestation arises.

If, in previous lives, one has not been perfumed by wholesome or unwholesome seeds, then in this present life, encountering the wholesome will not produce the wholesome, and encountering the unwholesome will not produce the unwholesome;

this is termed the "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) nature. Therefore, it is said that when wholesome and unwholesome objects confront the senses, they are assigned accordingly to their respective categories.
It is so. It is true. Furthermore, regarding "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), there are two meanings. First, the seeds of prior perfuming; this refers to the meaning previously discussed in the treatise.
Second, the seeds of new perfuming, which also has two aspects: first, the growth of seeds and manifestations through new perfuming;

second, the creation of seeds and manifestations for the future, which is why it is called "new perfuming. Regarding the growth of seeds and manifestations through new perfuming: it is like a person who has not yet drunk wine.
Although they find the taste pleasant, they do not wish to drink much; thus, the power of their seeds is not yet deep.

When that person is urged to drink more, the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) becomes great, such that daily they do not depart from the mental activity (*cittapracāra*) of drinking alcohol.

This constitutes the greatness of the power of the seeds, which increases through perfuming the manifest activity (*abhisamskāra*) of drinking alcohol; it is not a separate seed. And as for the drinking...
When alcohol manifests, it further perfumes the seeds, causing them to increase and grow so that they are difficult to sever throughout all time.

Just as the habitual tendencies of drinking alcohol cause both the seeds and the manifesting states to increase, so too do all afflictions—the manifesting states and seeds such as craving for wealth and craving for form—increase and persist without interruption over successive lifetimes. How truly lamentable! How tragic!
Were it not for the power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion in teaching these twenty-six afflictions—
the active seeds and various sufferings of saṃsāra— how could one possibly know their faults? Therefore,
all practitioners on the path of cultivation must, in every thought-moment, cultivate ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Only through the Path and other dharmas, as well as the six *pāramitās* and so forth, can one finally escape suffering (Alas!).

If one does not habitually cultivate practices such as the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom so that their seeds become powerful, what will one rely upon when the time of death approaches?
Therefore it is said: "Before the barrier of birth and death, even half-letters cannot provide mutual rescue. In short, there is filial piety...
Even one’s descendants cannot take its place. Regarding the statement that "nature, realm, and sensation constantly revolve and change":
nature refers to the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral; realm refers to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Therefore, one experiences these feelings of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Furthermore, at the beginning one receives them, and upon departing one relinquishes them;
thus they are called the "three feelings" or the "five feelings. As for their constant transformation:
led by wholesome seeds, one proceeds to the good realms of humans and devas; led by unwholesome seeds, one falls into the three miserable destinies. Hence, it is said that they are "constant."
"Transformation" means change.
Regarding the "root [afflictions] following faith and so forth," the general characteristics are discussed collectively as follows:
namely, the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), totaling twenty-six afflictions.

Regarding the mental factors (*caitta*), including the eleven wholesome mental factors, as well as the five universal, five object-specific, and four indeterminate factors, these internal and external categories are interconnected.

When proponents of the theory of correspondence argue that each of the first fifty-one mental factors is associated with all eight consciousnesses, they speak from the perspective of the majority of cases. Furthermore, each of these mental factors is also associated with the internal...
External connections and responses;
moving the body and uttering speech, thought alone is considered the foremost.
The treatise says: Question: It is said that the three types of action involve movement; why then is the action of volition (cetanā) considered the foremost? Answer: Movement...
The body moves because of mental volition (*cetanā*); speech is initiated because of mental volition.
Therefore, it is said here that what is most powerful is not the strength of body or speech, but rather the karma of volition and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone that is supreme.
Now, this volition has two meanings: first, deliberative volition (*abhyūha-cetanā*), when the mind is not yet settled; second, determinative volition (*niścaya-cetanā*).
Volition (*cetanā*) is decisiveness; it is so called because it cannot be altered.
Therefore, whether one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds, or even cultivates the supramundane path to realize the fruits of enlightenment, all are accomplished through the karma of volition.
Thus, it can be understood that the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is the most powerful.
Regarding the discussion on how projecting and completing karma exerts its power to draw forth results, the treatise asks:
"As for the wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions previously performed, it is not yet known what kind of fruit they will produce."
Answer: It refers to the fruit of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) and the fruit of completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*). Question: What is meant by the fruit of projecting karma? Answer:

Due to the manifestation of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—performed in previous lives, these are stored within the eighth consciousness by means of the seven consciousnesses, thereby forming the seeds of projecting karma.
These project [the self] into the present, drawing forth the fruits of the two retributions of suffering and pleasure. If...

If there were neither good nor evil, there would simply be no fruit. Therefore, regarding the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*): its cause may be either good or evil, but its fruit is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Good and evil are like flowers that bloom beforehand; as for the neutral, it is the flower of maturation (*vipāka*). This is because the fruit of maturation does not coincide with the performance of the karma itself.

Furthermore, regarding the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*), it may result in a person being born with a predisposition toward killing; although such a person is born in the human realm, they incur [retribution].
Regarding the maturation fruit of projecting karma, one may receive retribution such as a short lifespan or much illness, which does not accord with the aspirations of the six consciousnesses.
However, if during life one was fond of releasing living beings and cultivated thoughts of loving-kindness, then even within the human realm, one will obtain a long life and freedom from illness.
It summons the retribution of a strong and powerful body in order to fulfill the vow of the sixth consciousness; therefore, it constitutes a ripening karma (*niṣyanda-karma*).

Thus, among all other wholesome or unwholesome factors, one should know that in the world, nothing possesses greater power than the seeds of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), for they draw one toward the realms of gods, humans, asuras, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts.
Beings in the realm of ghosts or the realm of animals may be led to the heavens of the four dhyānas or the four formless absorptions.

If their retribution in the heavens of the four dhyānas or four formless absorptions is exhausted, their projecting karma (ākṣepaka-karma) may again lead them to the human realm; however, this occurs only if they have not committed evil karma that constitutes a new projection.
Furthermore, projecting karma also leads one to the retribution within the three evil realms. Thus, the eight consciousnesses are like a criminal;
projecting karma is like being conscripted into labor; and the six destinies are like various counties and districts. For this reason, the conscription by projecting karma is most powerful.
Why is this? It is because the eight consciousnesses, depending upon the seeds of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), each achieve their respective retributions (*vipāka*).

Therefore, projecting karma is the most powerful. Furthermore, it is like a person who cultivates morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom, or concurrently cultivates the causes for the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), or recites the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in a pure land;
in such cases, the power of these pure karmas is strong, yet the seventh consciousness—
Stored within the eight consciousnesses, it accomplishes the power of inconceivable pure karma.

It instantly empties the characteristics of the five aggregates and can swiftly lead one to the Western Pure Land, where the fruit of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is realized;

this is also due to the power of the seeds of such propelling karma. This is not a mundane seed of propelling karma, but rather a supramundane power of cultivated unconditioned cessation through analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*).
It is also merely a metaphor for "drawing forth the seed. The first chapter is concluded.
Next, the verse describes the initiation of the untainted [path] and the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), wherein innate afflictions still manifest as active entanglements and latent tendencies.
After the Ground of Far-reaching Travel, one is purely untainted; With observation perfectly clear and bright, one illuminates the great chiliocosm.
In the first of the four lines of this present treatise, it says:
"Having initiated the initial mind on the Ground of Joy, the innate [afflictions] still manifest as entanglements and latent tendencies."
The Treatise says: Since one is currently in the stage of ordinary sentient beings, how can there be the eight stages of the sages? The answer is:

Because in a previous life one encountered a supreme Mahāyāna spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and was thus perfumed with the most supreme, perfect, and sudden (yuan-dun) teaching, the seeds were powerfully established;
now, by being perfumed once again, the perfect and sudden teaching truly means that a single awakening is the awakening to all.
Therefore, when one seed of the discrimination of self-view is severed, all are severed; how could one not believe this?
Consequently, at the beginning of the eighth stage, one transcends the level of ordinary beings, enters the rank of Bodhisattvas, and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is only the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) that can be severed; however, the subtle, co-emergent seeds (*bīja*) are the most difficult to sever.
Therefore, it is said that even at the eighth fruit and the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), there still remain manifest entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Consequently, it is only from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the sixth stage that one completely severs the active afflictions that nourish rebirth (*janmopabṛṃhaṇa-kleśa*) as well as the seeds of ordinary worldly mind (*pṛthagjana-citta*). This is because [the seventh...]
The seeds of the noble vision (*ārya-darśana*) are severed precisely within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*); this can be understood from the subsequent text of the verse.
"The Stage of Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*) and beyond is purely untainted (*anāsrava*), Observing with perfect clarity, it illuminates the great trichiliocosm.
The Commentary states: "Far-reaching" means being far removed from the three realms (*tridhātu*). It is the ground that approaches the treasure-trove of the Dharma King. Therefore, prior to this—

Within the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one relies upon the stages of practice of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those of the three vehicles alike emerge from the burning house;
having traveled past three hundred *yojanas* and reached the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, they eventually arrive at the city of the Buddha-jewel.

It is there that they ride the great white ox-cart. Therefore, for those who have become free from outflows (*anāsrava*), within the category of the realization of the Way, there is no longer any outflow.
This is the fruition. Therefore, it is said that one is able to observe with perfect clarity, illuminating the great dharma-realm of the trichiliocosm.

As for the wisdom that performs this observation, because it reflects objects like a mirror without retaining any emotional attachment, its nature may be understood as being identical to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśana-jñāna*).
This has already been explained above. This concludes the preceding chapter on the fourfold classification of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Joining this with the previous section on ordinary worldly consciousness (*pṛthagjana-citta*) and the untainted, the entire major chapter is now complete; the commentary has finished its exposition.
Question: The six consciousnesses have already been clarified. Now, regarding the subtle meaning of the seventh consciousness, what is its function? Answer:
As for the function of the seventh consciousness, it takes the eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its object and acts upon itself.

Furthermore, it is associated with the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmika), the omnipresent factors (sarvatraga), the wisdom among the specific-objective factors (viśeṣa-bhūmika), and the four afflictions: self-delusion (ātma-moha), self-pride (ātma-māna), self-view (ātma-dṛṣṭi), and self-love (ātma-tṛṣṇā).
[This] will be discussed in detail in the following section. Question: By what name is *manas* designated? Answer: In this region [China], it is called "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*).

It is also called the "defiled-pure consciousness," and also the "discriminating consciousness. Regarding "defiled": because it is associated at every moment with the eight consciousnesses and the four afflictions, it is named the "defiled consciousness.
Furthermore, the six consciousnesses become outflowing and defiled at every moment; this is precisely the seventh consciousness.
Moment by moment, the six consciousnesses become tainted and defiled; moment by moment, the seventh consciousness becomes untainted and pure.

Therefore, it is called the "tainted-pure consciousness. Furthermore, if one distinguishes moment by moment that the conditioned is illusory and the unconditioned is empty, yet does not escape these two views, this is called the "discriminating consciousness. If one escapes these two views, then...
The Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) is so called because it accomplishes the Great Perfect Wisdom (mahāvaipulyajñāna). It is also termed the "transmitting consciousness" (saṃkrāntivijñāna);
just as when a person’s own strength is insufficient and they are busily occupied with miscellaneous tasks both internally and externally, it is therefore named the transmitting consciousness.
Because the Venerable Master Xuánzàng [also] provided twelve lines of verse regarding its causes within the context of the seven consciousnesses.

The third verse concerning the seventh consciousness is further divided into two parts (the first eight lines form the chapter on ordinary sentient beings; the latter four lines form the chapter on the fruit of sainthood).
The initial verse [concerning ordinary beings] states:

When accompanied by an object-substance (*saviṣaya*), it is obscured (*nivṛta*); it pervades both the mental state and its basis. Following conditions, it clings to a self; its mode of apprehension is erroneous.
The eight universal [mental factors] and the five object-determining ones are associated with wisdom; Greed, delusion, self-view, and pride are ever-present and follow along.
Constantly and thoroughly deliberating upon the aspect of "self," sentient beings are perpetually mired in confusion day and night.
The four afflictions and the eight universals arise in conjunction; The six evolving consciousnesses are called the basis for both defilement and purity.
Now, regarding the first of the eight propositions in this treatise, it says:
"That which involves a substantial basis (dai-zhi) and is obscured (you-fu) pertains to both the mental faculty (qing) and the fundamental [consciousness] (ben).

The treatise states: "Involving a substantial basis" means that the seeing-division (jian-fen) of the seven consciousnesses takes the internal seeing-division of the eighth consciousness as its object; therefore, it is said to involve a substantial basis.
The arising of internal and external views combines to produce a reflection that serves as an object; this is the "substantial basis" (zhì) of a nominal designation.

It consists purely of the seeing-aspects (jiàn-fēn) of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, produced together from their seeds, and is not produced by external objects of the five sense-dusts (wǔ-chén). Therefore, it is called an "object with a substantial basis" (dài-zhì jìng).

Because its substance consists of the subjective aspect (*vijñapti*) of the mind and mental factors (*caitta*), it is said that there are two types of "obscured" (*nivṛta*): first, obscured by nature;
second, non-obscured by nature. Regarding why both are designated as "non-defined" (*avyākṛta*) due to these two types of obscuration:

the seven consciousnesses grasp the eighth consciousness as a self, and are thus called "obscured-non-defined. Because the seventh consciousness does not grasp the eighth consciousness as a self, it is called [non-obscured-non-defined].
It is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). When it previously resided in the fourth dhyāna heaven and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), it was termed "obscured.
If it resides in the summit of the four formless heavens (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is termed "unobscured-unspecified" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Because it has extinguished the seeds of the seven consciousnesses, there is no objective referent (*sālambana*) that carries a substantial essence. Question: Since the seven consciousnesses have been extinguished and one no longer conceives of a self (*ātman*), why is this not the stage of a noble one (*ārya*)? Answer: Due to...
Although the seeds of the self, perfumed by ignorance, do not manifest due to the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this is because the seeds of the self do not appear;

it is not that the delusion regarding the nature [of reality] has been destroyed. If the delusion regarding the nature were destroyed, then all illusory objects—whether in a state of concentration or non-concentration—would be empty of self-nature.
Therefore, one never again conceives of a self, and only then does pure, wondrous wisdom arise. This is the eighth [stage], Non-arising. Thus...
This is the shell of indeterminate ignorance (*avyākṛta-avidyā*). Again, it was asked: "If it is obscured (*nivṛta*), why does it not constitute the nature of good or evil?
The answer is: "Because the seven consciousnesses do not range over external objects, they cannot produce seeds of good or evil; therefore, it is called 'indeterminate.

As for its pervading both the phenomenal and the fundamental, because the seventh consciousness clings to objects moment by moment, it takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as its sentient being."

The object is therefore called the fundamental basis of emotion common to the eight consciousnesses. It is not that the eight consciousnesses themselves are sentient beings; rather, they grasp the seventh consciousness as their emotional basis.
Following conditions, they cling to the measure of "self" as being real.
The Commentary says: How is it that the seven consciousnesses grasp the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness and thereby become non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)?

The answer is: Master Li said, "Sentiment arises and wisdom is separated. This refers to the sentiment of the seven consciousnesses; being deluded regarding the fundamental nature-wisdom (*prakṛti-jñāna*), they form the shell of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The transformation of appearances results in distinct entities; that is, the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses is originally the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness.

Fundamentally, it does not harbor emotions. However, due to the seventh consciousness, emotions arise in an instant. As the sixth consciousness performs discrimination, it undergoes a transformation of appearance that seems to carry a "substantial essence" (*saviṣaya-sadṛśa*), and thus becomes an object of non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).
Why is this so? Because the appearances before one's eyes are fundamentally empty from the outset, lacking even a single inch [of independent reality].
[If] it were obtainable as a thread, then to say now that it "has characteristics" would establish it as an object of non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). Question:

Previously it was stated that the two valid cognitions—direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)—are unerring, and thus there are no objects of non-valid cognition. Now, [you speak of] objects that are not erroneous according to these two valid cognitions, direct perception and inference.

How is it that [the seventh consciousness] becomes non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)? Answer: It becomes non-valid cognition when its objective conditions are erroneous; this is among the types of non-valid cognition.
Furthermore, it becomes non-valid cognition because it now relies on the actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), yet perceives "prior characteristics" (*pūrvanimitta*).

These are the non-valid cognitions resulting from the delusion of ignorance regarding the nature. Question: If the seven consciousnesses grasp the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as being non-valid cognition, then how does delusion arise through contact with external objects?
This too would constitute non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Would this not mean that both the internal and external [realms] are established as non-valid cognition?
Answer: The treatise states: "First, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); second, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); third, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The perfected nature is the meaning of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the dependent nature is the meaning of non-emptiness; and the imagined nature is the meaning of false delusion (*mṛṣā*). Furthermore, true emptiness...
This is the gate of non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpāda-aniruddha-mukha*). The meaning of "not empty" (*aśūnya*) is the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).

Due to delusion regarding the meanings of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing, the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established. Within the transformation of consciousness, it constitutes the *ālayavijñāna* and its two aspects—the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving (*darśana-bhāga*).

Furthermore, the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness is identical to the seeing-aspect of the five sensory consciousnesses, which takes the nature of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as its objective condition.

Regarding the objective aspect (viṣaya-nimitta-bhāga): delusion arises from contact with objects; one falsely discriminates the faculties, their objects, and the vessel-world (bhājana-loka), taking them to be substantially existent.
Therefore, the parikalpita-svabhāva is not a valid cognition (pramāṇa). This is because the *Xuánzǔ sòng* states: "The single word 'clinging' (*zhí*)."
This, then, subsumes the reckoning of the eight consciousnesses, both internal and external, and establishes them as objects that are not valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Therefore, people of today must understand that all matters in their ordinary daily lives are entirely objects of non-valid cognition; they are like dreams or illusions.

Regarding the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*’s discussion on the eight universal secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and their association with wisdom (*prajñā*), it asks: Why are the eight great secondary afflictions associated with the seven consciousnesses, and furthermore, why are they associated with the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and wisdom?
The answer is: Because the seven consciousnesses rely upon the six consciousnesses and rush outward, they constitute restlessness (*auddhatya*). Because...

The six consciousnesses are intermittent and subject to confusion and delusion, whereas the seventh consciousness is uninterrupted and takes the internal as its object; therefore, it is associated with torpor (*styāna*).

Due to the unfitness (*akarmanyatā*) of the seventh consciousness, there arise lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).
Consequently, these eight great secondary afflictions are universally associated with the seventh consciousness; thus, for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are external...
This is common to all those who follow the Hīnayāna. Thus, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Kāśyapa and others said: "At that time, I was sitting in the assembly;
my body was weary and exhausted, and I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, not believing that there is a Mahāyāna or that a Buddha could be attained."

This is immediately proximate to the eight major derivative afflictions (*anuvyañjana-kleśa*), yet it is not itself an affliction. Furthermore, regarding that which is associated with the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*):

because the seventh consciousness relies upon the external objects of the six consciousnesses, the universal factors are associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, as well as being associated with the seventh and eighth consciousnesses in every moment.
If the six consciousnesses do not take external objects as their conditions, then the seventh consciousness would have no basis for its objective support (*ālambana*). In total...

Taking the objects of the eight consciousnesses as their conditions, these five universal mental factors (pañca-sarvatraga-caitta) are associated with the seventh consciousness at every moment. Question:
Since they are already associated with the eighth consciousness, how can they be associated with the seventh consciousness? Answer:

The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the seventh consciousness arises from the same seeds as the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness. Therefore, the five universal factors of the eighth consciousness are precisely the five mental factors of the seventh consciousness.
This is what is shared [by all]. Furthermore, regarding that which is associated with the discernment (*prajñā*) among the object-specific mental states:

when followers of external paths enter the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) up to the realms of the four formless heavens, at the moment the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object, it is indeed associated with false discernment.
However, once ignorance and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) are destroyed, it is associated with correct discernment.
Regarding the treatise on the concomitance of greed, delusion, the view of self, and pride:
how are these four afflictions of the seventh consciousness the same as the four afflictions of the eighth consciousness in terms of arising from the same seeds? The answer is:
Within the eighth consciousness, there are four afflictions—self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*)—which are associated with it.

These four afflictions only come into being through the grasping of the seven consciousnesses. Why is this? Because of the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one grasps internal and external objects as truly existent;
therefore, it is called self-delusion. "Delusion" means confusion. This delusive nature-seed is stored within the eighth consciousness.
This causes the seven consciousnesses to grasp at a self and give rise to pride (*māna*). Due to this pride, views (*dṛṣṭi*) are formed.
Because views are formed, contact with objects gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Due to craving, various karmas are created.

Therefore, it is generally because the nature of delusion consists of the view of self that the seven consciousnesses grasp the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness and remain in constant association with the four afflictions at every moment.
Now, the verse states: "The character 'greed' (tan) is actually the character 'craving' (ai). It is the character 'greed' that is used merely because the level and oblique tones do not harmonize.
This refers to the four afflictions of the seven consciousnesses accompanying the eight consciousnesses."

Regarding the phrase "constantly and thoroughly deliberating" (*nitya-parīkṣā*) as it pertains to the characteristic of the self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), the commentary states that there are four categories of distinction: First, that which is constant but not thorough, such as the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because it lacks investigative discernment (*parīkṣā*).
Second, that which is thorough but not constant, such as the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which, although it possesses investigative discernment, is not constant.
It is constant; however, because it is interrupted when encountering states of non-mentation, it is not [always] present. The third type is neither investigative nor constant.

For example, the first five consciousnesses perceive objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and are thus non-conceptual; hence they are said to be "non-investigative. They flow momentarily within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Therefore, it is said that [the seventh consciousness] is not constant. Fourth, within the present seven consciousnesses, it is both discerning and constant.

Because it possesses discernment both internally and externally, and because it is constant from moment to moment without interruption, it is said to be "both discerning and constant. The present verse states:
"Constantly and discerningly it deliberates, following along with the notion of self. Because it clings to the eighth consciousness as the self, it is said to "follow along."
Sentient beings are perpetually deluded day and night.

The Commentary states: Sentient beings, including those in the realms of form and formlessness, possess a nature that is moment-to-moment deluded throughout the day and night, whereby they cling to a self.
It is only after the path of the Tathāgata’s vajra that they finally escape this fruit of suffering.
Regarding the treatise on the arising of the four delusions and the eight great [afflictions] in conjunction,
it says: As for the current statement "deluded regarding the four kinds," although the four delusions were previously distinguished in the preceding verse,

they are here combined and referred to as "the four delusions" because delusion arises from the seeds of affliction within, and delusion subsequently arises in contact with external objects, resulting in the formation of views and craving.

This continues until the eight great [consciousnesses] arise in mutual correspondence with the internal and external; therefore, it does not refer solely to the seven consciousnesses, but rather speaks of their correspondence with the eight great ones.

If one is deluded regarding the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) and attains liberation from even one, then the internal and external are suddenly empty of illusory appearances, and one perceives the Dharma-body.
The sixth transformation is called the basis for defilement and purification.
The Treatise asks: How do the six consciousnesses act as the seventh consciousness in terms of defilement and purification? The answer is:

Because the six consciousnesses take the preceding five sensory objects as their nature-objects (*viṣaya*), they give rise to minds of liking and disliking, attachment and aversion, or they perceive what is wholesome and love it.

One cultivates goodness regarding objects. Seeing their unwholesome nature, one loathes them and resolves to abandon them moment by moment. By means of the six consciousnesses, one achieves purity and severs delusions;
this causes the seventh consciousness to likewise achieve purity and sever delusions. These [impressions] are infused and gathered within the eighth consciousness, where they are stored.
Thus, they form the seeds of projecting karma that will inevitably lead to the attainment of future untainted, supramundane fruits.
If objects such as likes and dislikes arise, this is an unwholesome mind. Moment by moment, one must create [karma];
through the six consciousnesses, defilement is established, increasing present karma. This causes the seventh consciousness to also become defiled in nature, which perfumes the eighth consciousness;
it gathers and stores [this karma], thereby forming seeds of projecting karma that lead to the experience of various bitter fruits of suffering in the future.
[The text continues with] "Ear. Question: Why is it that the seventh consciousness depends upon the six consciousnesses to become defiled or pure? Answer:
Because the seventh consciousness lacks the power to create [its own state], it must generally depend on the power of the six consciousnesses to be established.

It is like a mother who, lacking strength, must depend on her son's strength to accomplish [her purpose]. Thus concludes the eight-line verse concerning ordinary sentiment (*pṛthagjana*) as discussed above.
The next verse [states]:
"The nature of equality in the initial moment of the Stage of Supreme Joy, which is the fruit of the Sage;
my constant destruction of effortless conduct, manifested by the Tathāgata as the Body of Enjoyment for Others, is the object for Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages."
Now, regarding the first of the four propositions in this treatise, it states:
"The nature of equality in the initial moment of supreme joy.

The *Treatise* says: "In the chapter on the five sensory consciousnesses and the sixth consciousness, [the stage] is generally based on the initial mind as the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Now, furthermore—

What is meant by “relying on the first stage, the Stage of Joy”? The answer is: according to the intention of the Great Patriarch (Dōgen), one must first individually recognize the eight phrases of the "Chapter on Ordinary Sentiments" (*Fanjōshō*).

Only when the meaning of the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*Shōmetsumon*) has been thoroughly exhausted can the [Gate of] Suchness (*Shinnyomon*) be suddenly revealed and established as the "Three Realms are Mind-Only.
Now, that which is "Mind-Only" is precisely the Gate of Suchness. Therefore, the aforementioned Gate of Arising and Ceasing is understood through this knowledge.
The myriad dharmas are but the perception of consciousness. Later, regarding "mind-only," not even the slightest dharma is to be attained.
If one directly points to the single mind and understands it with immediate clarity, one enters the first stage (bhūmi). Proceeding thus up to the seventh stage, one enters the eighth stage.
One then employs the eight kinds of wondrous views of non-arising and enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata’s wondrous fruition.

Regarding the statement, "I constantly refute [those who hold to] effortless practice" (*anābhoga-caryā*): what stage is attained through this effortlessness? Why is it not said that one refutes the Dharma? And...

He asked, "Do you say that I am constantly suppressing? He replied, "One who is without effort (*anābhoga*) remains within the seven stages, where in every thought-moment the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*) has not yet ceased.
Now, having reached the eighth stage, one suddenly transcends the wisdom of signless contemplation, such that it never arises again."
However, although the aspect of wisdom has been liberated, it is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because seeing has not yet been relinquished.

Although the seeds of self have been completely exhausted, a slight residue of attachment to phenomena still remains. If one were to suddenly relinquish [this] and enter the ocean of the Dharma-realm, one would universally manifest emanations.
Being sovereign and unimpeded, one is completely liberated from both the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena; only then does one truly attain the constant destruction of phenomena.
Therefore, in this passage, it simply says "the constant destruction of the self."
The Tathāgata manifests the Enjoyment Body for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), which serves as the object for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
The treatise asks: Why is it said that the Tathāgata manifests the Enjoyment Body for Others, rather than the Enjoyment Body for Self (*svasaṃbhogakāya*)? The answer is as follows:

The Tathāgata inherently possesses the bliss of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*). It is for the sake of those bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as their spiritual capacity that he manifests the body of other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
Furthermore, it was asked: "Is the manifestation of the sixteen-foot golden body considered the body of other-enjoyment?
Or is it the manifestation of bodies with the ocean-like marks of atoms that constitutes the body of enjoyment? The answer is: The Tathāgata does not [manifest] by means of marks...
Its essence is merely signless quiescence. Yet, the Dharma-body is fully endowed with marks and majestic deportment, such that all beings in the world may behold it according to their inclinations.

For this reason, it may manifest as a great fullness pervading empty space, or again manifest as a hundred billion minor transformation bodies, or as an ocean of subtle dust-like marks, or as an inexhaustible cloud of bodies. How could these [bodies] for the enjoyment of others be...?
Regarding "conceivable": as for the self-enjoyment body, it is solely the one true, pure Dharma-realm.
This concludes the preceding chapter on the untainted fruit. Thus, the first major section, which summarizes both ordinary worldly sentiments and the untainted fruit, is completed.
Question: The seven consciousnesses have already been clarified; however, the eighth consciousness remains obscure and subtle. How, then, can it be known? Answer: In Sanskrit it is called *ālaya*;
in this land [of China], it is termed the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*). It is so named because it is able to store all phenomena (*dharmas*) as well as their seeds.

As for "all phenomena," these refer to the sense organs, their objects, and the physical world. Furthermore, it is able to store the manifestations of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.

Because it consists of both the formations (*saṃskāra*) and the seeds (*bīja*), it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. It is also called "the non-perishing consciousness" (*avipraṇāśa-vijñāna*), because within the cycle of the six realms of existence, it cannot perish.
Master Xuangzuo, among the eight consciousnesses, further provides twelve lines of verse: [Verse omitted] Master Xuangzuo, among the eight consciousnesses, further provides twelve lines of verse:
[verse follows].

The fourth section on the eight consciousnesses is further divided into two parts (the first eight lines constitute the Chapter on Ordinary Sentient Beings; the final four lines constitute the Chapter on the Fruit of Sagehood).
The first verse concerns the nature of ordinary sentient beings:
Their nature is exclusively non-obscured [neutral], possessing five universal mental factors; They arise according to other [conditions] and by the power of karma, across various realms and stages.
The Two Vehicles fail to understand this due to deluded attachments; Because of this, they can engage in vast disputes with the Master of Treatises.
The Three Piṭakas are inexhaustible, Profound as a deep pool with seven waves stirred by the wind of objects.
It perfumes and sustains the seeds within the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world; Leaving first and arriving last, it acts as the presiding lord.
Now, regarding the first of the eight propositions in this treatise, it says:
"Its nature is exclusively non-obscured and universally present among the five [mental factors].
The commentary states: "Nature" refers to the indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature among the three natures, because it does not coexist with the afflictions within the preceding seven consciousnesses.

Because they coexist; furthermore, because within the state of equality there is no opposition or resistance, as the cause encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome while the fruit is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Moreover, because the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) within the eight consciousnesses is devoid of conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*), the seeing-portion of the internal consciousness is identical to the external seeing-portion of the five consciousnesses.
Therefore, when the five consciousnesses perceive objective spheres (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), they constitute direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a non-conceptual object.
This refers to that very [eighth consciousness].
Furthermore, the eighth consciousness can only contain and store (ālaya), but cannot be grasped as a self (ātmagrāha).

Therefore, the first seven consciousnesses, moment by moment, act as the perfuming agents (vāsaka), while the eighth consciousness, moment by moment, receives perfuming as the perfumed object (vāsya). Thus, the seven consciousnesses—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—[are all capable of perfuming].
The three natures (trisvabhāva) are able to store within the eight consciousnesses as the seeds that function as projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).

As for those of the unobscured nature (*anivṛta*), this has already been discussed previously. Regarding what are called the five omnipresent mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*), they are collectively associated with the eight consciousnesses at every moment.
This extends even to the realm of the four formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*), where they still correspond with five mental factors (*caitta*), whether manifest or latent.
This is as stated regarding the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Such is the case.

Regarding the theory that the realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*) arise according to the power of the karma of others, the treatise states: "Realms" refers to the three realms; "stages" refers to the nine stages. This occurs due to the power of the seeds of propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) within the eight consciousnesses.
It leads [the being] into the realm of desire, to the ground where the five destinies dwell together; it further leads them to the abodes of the four dhyānas and the four formless heavens.
Thus, the eighth consciousness, impelled by the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karmic forces, is led to the nine stages within the three realms.
That beings are born in their respective locations is entirely due to the power of these seeds.
The two vehicles do not realize this because they are deluded by attachment; for this reason, they are able to engage in debate with the Master of Treatises, who asks:
"In what way do the two vehicles fail to realize that there is an eighth consciousness which gives rise to deluded attachment? Answer:
Because śrāvakas and others know only that the six consciousnesses serve as the fundamental basis for defilement and purity. As for those who are defiled, they possess greed.

Due to hatred and delusion. "By means of purity" refers to possessing morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). The three realms constitute the sphere of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Greed, hatred, and delusion, etc., constitute its Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Morality, concentration, wisdom, and so forth, constitute its Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

The supramundane *nirvāṇa* of unconditioned nature constitutes its Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). This is because one investigates the cause of the fruit of suffering: from what source does it arise?

[It] comes about: through the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), such as greed, hatred, and delusion, the fruit of suffering is produced. Furthermore, from what does the fruit of the bliss of *nirvāṇa* arise?

It is only by cultivating the causes of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), that the supramundane fruit of *nirvāṇa* is achieved.
Nevertheless, this formation of defilement is fundamentally based upon the six consciousnesses; therefore, now [the text discusses] the Great...
Regarding the statement that the eighth consciousness is identical to the Tathāgatagarbha within the vehicle of the Śrāvakas: this is not accepted.
Therefore, it is said that because the views of the Hīnayāna are shallow, they engage in polemical debate with the Mahāyāna.
The *Hao-hao Sanzang Bukeqiong Lun* states:

"Vast and expansive" (*hao-hao*) refers to profound meaning. The "Three Pitakas" (*sanzang*) refer to the "that which can store," the "that which is stored," and the "that which is clung to as a store."

First, regarding "that which can store" (*ālaya*): it is discussed from the perspective of the sense of "maintaining," because it maintains and stores all seeds that have been perfumed by the manifestation of all phenomena.
Second, regarding "that which is stored": it is called "stored" from the perspective of the sense of "receiving perfuming."

It receives the seeds of the manifest virtuous and non-virtuous actions produced by the first six consciousnesses; through the seventh consciousness, it stores these within the eighth consciousness to form the seeds of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*).
Because it is perfumed by the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses, it is called the "threefold storehouse" (*trividha-ālaya*):

in terms of its function as "grasping and maintaining," the seventh consciousness grasps the internal seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as a self, thereby constituting the "self."
Delusion (*moha*), and so forth, up to the four afflictions such as self-love (*ātmasneha*), are fully associated [with the mind].
Furthermore, because the manifest [afflictions] act like a mother in producing seeds, they are the perfumers (*vāsaka*); the eight consciousnesses are the perfumed (*vāsya*).
If seeds produce manifest states, then since the seeds are the mothers of the manifest states, the manifest states are the children; thus, they mutually perfume one another.
Through habituation, it increases moment by moment without interruption; thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "It is the characteristic of boundless origination.

Therefore, the seed is what constitutes the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance, for it lies dormant within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), conforming to the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, that which constitutes the inconceivable perfuming (*vāsanā*) and becomes the seed for the fruit to be drawn forth in the future is precisely what constitutes its inconceivable transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Moreover, regarding latent ignorance (*anuśaya-avidyā*), there are three types: first, the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*janmābhiṣyandana-avidyā*).
This is precisely the seed of self-love (*ātma-sneha*), which is subsumed within the eight consciousnesses.

It is completely severed from the first through the sixth grounds, as well as by those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) at the sixth ground, such that it never arises again. Second, the ignorance of the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha-avidyā*) is severed upon advancing from the sixth ground to the seventh, entering the eighth ground;
here, both [bodhisattvas] and those of the two vehicles equally abandon the obstacles of the dual clinging to self and phenomena, and equally abandon them.

The view that obstructs the dharma of non-arising enters the ocean of the Dharma-realm; it is like the moon reflecting in ten thousand rivers, for it manifests infinite bodies to deliver sentient beings.
Third is the ignorance of the final stage, which is severed at the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages.

This consists of karma, the evolving [consciousness], and manifestation: karma serves as the seed, the evolving [consciousness] constitutes the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*), and manifestation constitutes the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*).
It is not severed within the segmented *vipāka-phala* (fruition of maturation). Why?

Because the seventh and eighth stages have already long since severed the worldly, outflowing (*sāsrava*), segmented birth-and-death that is the fruition of maturation. What is severed now is described as follows:

at the eighth stage, one severs the "manifest aspect" (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*), thereby permanently relinquishing the "objective aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*); at the ninth stage, one severs the "transformative aspect" (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), thereby permanently relinquishing the "subjective aspect" (*darśana-bhāga*).
[This is] the division. At the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), one abandons the characteristics of karma, which is the permanent relinquishing of the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, there remains a final subtle seed that is abandoned within the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*). This is the characteristic of the fruit of supramundane, untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*).

It is precisely the fruit of supramundane transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāmikī-jarāmaraṇa*). It is also called the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*). Therefore, it is said: "Immediately after the diamond-like path..."
The emptiness of the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is precisely the relinquishing of the fruits of the two types of death. Again, it was asked:
"Within the fruit of the Tathāgata, does the nature of the *ālaya-vijñāna* as a ripening fruit exist, or does the ripening fruit not exist? He replied: "There is no ripening fruit.
It was asked: "How is it that various Mahāyāna sūtras state that the Tathāgata cultivated immeasurable hardships in the past..."
One practices asceticism and now attains the fruits such as the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses;
is this not the experience of the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*)? Answer: Have you not seen it stated in the sutras: "This body of mine is none other than the eternally abiding Dharma-body"?
It is further said: "The nature of the self has never existed; that which belongs to the self is likewise empty and quiescent. How then could the Tathāgatas possess a physical body?
Truly, there is no fruit of karmic maturation; there is only the nature of the Dharma-body. It is also said:
"Perfect enlightenment returns to non-attainment"—this is it.
"The abyss is deep; the seven waves have the objective realm as their wind. The Treatise says:
"The abyss of the eight consciousnesses" refers to the fact that the eight consciousnesses sustain all minds and their respective objects without ceasing;
this is why it is called an abyss. It is like the great ocean, profoundly still and ever tranquil, yet [it is stirred] by being affected with... [ignorance].
The winds of the five sensory objects stir up the waves of the seven consciousnesses, forming the surges of the six consciousnesses.

Moment by moment, without interruption, wholesome and unwholesome states manifest, affecting both the active seeds and the latent seeds; thus, one transmigrates through the three realms forever without end.
How truly lamentable this is! Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* is ever-abiding; moved by the winds of objective conditions, its various..."
The waves of the various consciousnesses surge forth and arise. It is further said: "For example, like the great ocean’s waves, there are no distinct characteristics;
so it is with the mind of the various consciousnesses—difference and unity cannot be found.

The former verse states that [the mind] is driven by the winds of ignorance and the objects of the five sense-dusts, and thus the waves of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses arise. The latter verse suddenly shatters ignorance.
Because it is subject to the winds of objective conditions and the characteristics of manifesting seeds, it is said: "There are no various characteristics;
nothing distinct from the One can be found; it is solely the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body."

Regarding the discussion on how [the eighth consciousness] receives perfuming and maintains the seeds of the root-body and the vessel-world, the *Treatise* states: "As for receiving perfuming and maintaining the seeds:

by means of the seeds of the wholesome and unwholesome active manifestations of the preceding seven consciousnesses experienced in previous lives, the seeds of the propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) of the eight consciousnesses are formed. These propel [the continuum] into the present and future, thereby forming the root-body."

The immediate objective parts (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*) within the eight consciousnesses are the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*); these are the remote objective parts (*viprakṛṣṭa-nimitta-bhāga*) within the eight consciousnesses.

Because these internal and external, immediate and remote objective parts are all sustained by the seeds of the eighth *ālayavijñāna*, "seeds" refers here to the seeds of the propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) from previous lives, which are also the seeds for our present life-force (*jīvitendriya*). They sustain and maintain them.

The body does not disintegrate. Should one encounter external conditions that cause fainting or the suspension of breath, if the seeds of the life-faculty driven by projecting karma are not severed, the body will be sustained for three days, five days, or even up to seven days, such that the physical form composed of the four great elements does not scatter.
Therefore, it is credible that the seeds of propelling karma possess such power.
Regarding the discourse on "the one who goes before and comes after acting as the master":
[Question] Since the eight consciousnesses come first, what is their appearance? And when they depart later, what is their appearance? [Answer] First...
As for "coming," it refers to the seeds of the propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) from previous lives drawing forth the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Through the combination of the father’s semen, the mother’s blood, and the drawn-in seeds of one's own spiritual essence—these three factors in union—the embryo is formed.

After seven times seven, or forty-nine days, the physical basis of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) is completed. Furthermore, within the womb, there arise the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and gallbladder.

From the hair, fur, nails, and teeth, down to the mind, intellect, and consciousness—there is not a single item that is not clearly distinguished, extending even to the characteristics of old age and death, or the fruits of suffering and pleasure; none are omitted. This is what is meant by the "signs of coming."
What is the characteristic of departing? By means of the eight consciousnesses, first the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the sixth and seventh consciousnesses depart.
The substance of the ālayavijñāna then takes on a semblance of wood or stone;
the entire body becomes cold, and only the seeds of the propelling karma remain, leading one to the various realms of the six destinies. This must be known. How is it known?
The Treatise says: "For the sages, it is at the crown; for those born in the heavens, it is in the eyes; for humans, it is in the heart; for hungry ghosts, it is in the abdomen;

for animals, it is at the knees; and for those in hell, it emerges from the soles of the feet. These are the signs of departure. Regarding "for the sages, it is at the crown": the entire body becomes cold, yet only the crown of the head remains warmest.
Or, regarding those born in the heavens: because the entire body is cold, only the eyes on the face remain warm. This continues down to [the case of] hell...
Regarding "the footboard of the hell emerges": this refers to the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), which projects one toward the realm of the hells.

The entire body becomes cold, yet only the footboard remains warm. Question: If the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the retributive body (*vipāka-deha*) must be relinquished, does this not imply that there are phenomena external to the mind?
It would not be "mind-only" (*cittamātra*). Answer: The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states that there are four kinds of empty mirrors.
It is equal to empty space. First is the mirror of emptiness; second is the mirror of non-emptiness; third is the mirror of perfuming;
and fourth is the mirror of the emergence of dharmas. What is meant by the mirror of emptiness? It is because it is not associated with any arising, ceasing, or defiled dharmas.
What is meant by the mirror of non-emptiness? All dharmas abide within this mirror of emptiness, neither emerging nor...
It enters [into the nature of reality], because it eternally abides in a single nature. Why is it called the mirror of perfuming?

Because by means of cultivating all immeasurable wholesome dharmas, such as morality, concentration, and wisdom, one is perfumed so as to achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajña-jñāna*).
Why is it called the mirror of the emergence of the Dharma? Because all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are simultaneously severed and exhausted.

Therefore, because even the seeds of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been simultaneously liberated and exhausted, the ordinary mind within the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) likewise possesses the four meanings of a mirror.

First is the "empty mirror. Because all prior and subsequent reflections of the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) do not correspond with the mirror of emptiness-nature, for what reason would one [perceive] the characteristics of all maturation fruits?
First, these are illusory reflections, resembling images in an empty mirror; because they do not correspond with the essential nature of the empty mirror, [they are unreal].
Second, although there are reflections of the marks of maturation within the nature of the non-empty mirror, they neither emerge nor enter it;
therefore, when they come, there is no increase, and when they go, there is no decrease, for like the reflections in an empty mirror, they have no coming or going. Third, the perfuming...

Regarding the Mirror of Habituation: as stated in the subsequent chapter on the Untainted (*anāsrava*), if the seeds were not formed through the perfuming of untainted, inconceivable, and pure karma, how could the pure and wondrous fruit of a Tathāgata be accomplished? Regarding the Mirror of Transcendence through the Four Dharmas:

as stated in the eightfold chapter on the tainted states of ordinary beings, if one does not exhaustively investigate the gate of arising and ceasing wherein all phenomena are but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), then...
The principle of Mind-Only is likewise not manifest [as a separate entity]. Therefore, it is said that the Dharma is the nature of liberation and a mirror.

Thus, the four mirrors are perfected, and nature and characteristics are mutually fused; this is the wondrous meaning of Mind-Only. Consequently, outside of the mind, there are absolutely no phenomena whatsoever.
Whoever perceives all phenomena perceives only the mind; how could there be any characteristics of maturation, coming, or going?
Therefore, it is said that the "master" is the power of the seeds drawn forth by good and evil, which acts as the master.
If those who exhaust the fruits induced by outflows were to do so, there would be nothing in the three realms that could bind them.
The preceding discussion on the eight phrases concerning the chapter on outflows is hereby concluded.
Next follows the verse on the chapter on the fruits of the noble ones among the noble.
Just before the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), one merely abandons the storehouse;

after the Vajra Path, the ripening consciousness becomes empty, and the Great Perfectly Pure [Wisdom] arises simultaneously. It shines universally throughout the lands and atoms of the ten directions.
Now, regarding the first of the four lines of this treatise, it says:
"Before the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), one merely abandons the storehouse; after the Vajra Path, the maturation (*vipāka*) is empty.
The treatise asks: "How is it that within the Immovable [Ground] one merely abandons the storehouse, and only after the Vajra Path does one first attain the emptiness of the maturation fruit?
The answer is given in the treatise: "From the outflowing causes (*sāsrava-hetu*) to the outflow-free fruits (*anāsrava-phala*), there are briefly three stages."
First is the stage of being clung to as "I" (*ātma-grāha-abhiniveśa*), which corresponds to the afflictions that moisten rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*).

Second is the stage of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma, which refers to the seeds produced by projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) that bring about the manifestation of karma; this is the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*prātibhāṣika-vaipakṣika-jāti-maraṇa*) consisting of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arising through co-nascence (*sahaja*).
Third is the stage of continuous maintenance, which refers to the fruit of the seeds of projecting karma. Furthermore, the treatise states: "If one cuts off the moisture..."
When one gives rise to the affliction of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), one first transcends the fourth stage (*bhūmi*). Upon entering the sixth stage, one becomes fully proficient;

at this point, the seeds of craving that moisten rebirth and the seeds of the four delusions (*kleśa*) within the eight consciousnesses are simultaneously severed. Furthermore, one destroys the nature of the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) as a composite whole and attains the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).
Second, regarding the stage of the fruits of good and evil karma: one cuts off birth-and-death through limited segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*).
Regarding the fruit: as in the first bhūmi, one first severs the obstacles of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and never again undergoes the fruit of an ordinary being within the four evil destinies.

From the second bhūmi onward, up until entering the eighth bhūmi, one suddenly sheds the karmic fruits of segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*) within the three realms, relinquishing the karmic fruits of the final body within the three realms—just as it is said:
"exhausting this present retribution-body" (together with those born simultaneously).

This is the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Regarding the stage of maintaining the three continuities, "severing the seeds of projecting karma" is as previously explained regarding the severance of分段生死 (paricchinna-janma-maraṇa, limited birth-and-death).
Upon transcending the mundane world, one immediately attains the power of wisdom from pure karma and receives a *nirmāṇakāya* (transformative body), which likewise is not severed.

Although this generally pertains to the *dharmakāya*, one still receives a *jñānakāya* (wisdom-body); yet, there are still traces of the characteristics of arising and ceasing within that wisdom, which have not yet been eliminated.
It is exhausted; therefore, it is called the "body that undergoes transformation" (*pariṇāmikakāya*). This is what is induced by inconceivable pure karma;

it is not the fruit of wholesome karma belonging to the desire realm or the form realm. Now, when one reaches the stage of the Tathāgata’s fruition, the wisdom of the body of transformation is finally and completely liberated.
After the perfection of the Vajra Path, there is not the slightest dharma to be attained; [this] definitively severs transformation.

It is easy. It is the emptiness of the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*). It is not merely that the ripening fruit within the three realms is empty; therefore, it is said that the two deaths are forever extinguished.
This is what is meant by "establishing oneself on the shore of the three virtues."
The Great Perfect Circle, stainless, arises simultaneously, Universally illuminating the lands within the dust motes of the ten directions.
The Treatise says: "The Great Perfect Circle" refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature). Because it responds immediately upon being invoked, it is called "wisdom.
Therefore, this wisdom exhausts the three periods of time without a single moment's interval, pervading the blossoms of the ten directions.
In the end, there is not even an inch of thread upon which to establish anything. Because it exists as something "subtly persistent," its application is effortless;

this is the primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Since it forever abandons the marks of arising and ceasing, it is like a mirror reflecting images without retaining any emotional attachment.

If it responds to external objects, it is termed the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); these are the provisional wisdoms (*upāya-jñāna*).
Whether it be appropriate or inappropriate, there is eternally no increase or decrease; this is called the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

Pervading the entire Dharma-realm and extending to the end of the future, it is fundamentally identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and lacks any characteristic of wisdom; this is called the Great Perfect Wisdom (*mahāpūrṇajñāna*).

Because its illuminating function is sovereign, it is metaphorically termed the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); yet, no actual characteristic of wisdom can be apprehended therein. Therefore, it is said: "There is neither wisdom, nor is there non-wisdom."
As for "attainment": it is the attainment of the stainless eye that universally reflects within every atom and every land throughout the ten directions.
By means of inexhaustible clouds of bodies—like the moon reflected in ten thousand rivers—it continues until the end of the future; therefore, it is said that they "arise simultaneously."
Because it does not come or go; because it is utterly quiescent. If the seed-syllable *A* is not a conventional designation, it is not an object of intellectual vision;
it is neither internal nor external; it is neither large nor small; it is neither one nor many. Therefore, when it functions, it is the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*);
when it abides in its essential nature, it is the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). Furthermore, wisdom is fundamentally the Dharma, and the Dharma is fundamentally wisdom. It is not—
It is neither one nor two; it is neither different nor identical. It is merely a matter of verbal expression, and both [views] result in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Thus, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra praised the Buddha in verse: "The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body is peerless throughout all the three realms."
Because it transcends the worldly path of language, its nature is neither existent nor non-existent;
therefore, even those who could count the moments of thought within the atoms of all lands cannot fathom it. It is simply the Tathāgata’s body of the pure dharma-realm.
