General Discussion of the Eight Consciousnesses: Dispelling Delusion to Realize the Nature of Wisdom.
Postscript: I have heard it said: "That which is the illusory body is, in fact, the Dharma-body. Now, that which is called the illusory body is [in truth] the *li*" (ordinary sentient beings).
It is the direct objective aspect (sākṣāt-bhāga) held within the ālayavijñāna. To the question, "By what is it formed? the answer is:
"Due to the power of the seeds of propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) from previous lives, it draws forth the seeds of good and evil from those past lives."
Thus, throughout this present life, one forms a phantom body (*māyā-deha*) that is the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the four great elements.

To begin with, as for this phantom body, it is like a magician who, by the power of incantations, conjures a phantom body consisting of the six sense faculties, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses.
If the incantation of the projecting karma from previous lives ceases, then the karmic characteristics of the phantom body will be cast off and come to rest.
Thus, although the illusory body may perish, only the wisdom of its nature does not perish. Why is this?

Because within the primordial wisdom-nature, all illusory appearances are non-corresponding with coming and going. Although these appearances manifest now, the essential substance of the illusory appearances is fundamentally empty from the beginning.
Why, then, must one eliminate those illusory appearances to reveal the Dharmakāya?
This is the very essence of emptiness. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This body of mine is now the eternally abiding Dharma-body;
thus, its coming is like the moon reflected in water, and its departing is like a magical illusion or a breath. It does not increase when it comes, nor does it decrease when it goes.

Being identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), how could there be any characteristics of a phantom body to be found within or without, even so much as a single thread?"
"How extraordinary! Someone asked him: 'If the self-nature of sentient beings is fundamentally and eternally abiding, why do they become deluded regarding it?
He replied: 'How profound is this question! What you ask concerns the cognitive nature of sentient beings; how could they be deluded about it?
Have you not heard the Sage say: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are mind-only"? "
"Consciousness is mind alone" refers to the mind of True Suchness (tathatā). Thus, the Awakening of Faith by Aśvaghoṣa states:
"All dharmas that are perceived are themselves the perception of the mind. Therefore, outside of the mind, there are no dharmas whatsoever.
Because it is mind-only; because all dharma-realms are primordially and eternally abiding, without transition or change.
Furthermore, by what cause do all dharmas exist? Answer: They are that which is seen by the mind of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). Therefore, one should know this.

Through the fundamental wisdom (*prakṛti-jñāna*), delusion becomes consciousness (*vijñāna*); through the delusion of consciousness, one is deluded regarding the nature; through the nature, form (*rūpa*) is established; through form, defilement (*saṃkleśa*) arises;

through defilement, falsehood (*mṛṣā*) is established; and through falsehood, grasping (*upādāna*) is established. Furthermore, falsehood acts as the grasper (*grāhaka*), while form serves as the grasped (*grāhya*).
It is like the deluded mind of a drunkard, whereby all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) are produced from within the absence of phenomena (*adharma*). Thus it is said.
Within the state of no-mind, all minds are accomplished. That which is "without dharma" is the fundamental nature;
that which is "without mind" is fundamental wisdom. Furthermore, this fundamental wisdom is quiescent illumination; it is the immovable wisdom of our own fundamental nature.
Therefore, if sentient beings do not become deluded regarding the nature of wisdom within the present moment, their consciousness will immediately become wisdom.
Form itself constitutes the nature. That which is the form-body is the dharma-body. Therefore, when encountering objects, there is clarity and suchness, for there is no sound or form.
All that is seen as phenomena is merely mind, because it is what is manifested by the mind of true suchness;
though seen, it is not seeing. Thus, the five consciousnesses are the wisdom within the nature of the dharma-body.
Since the light of wisdom within the nature of the Dharma-body itself reflects like a mirror, it is both responsive and non-responsive.

Being non-responsive, it constitutes the wisdom within the perfected nature; being responsive without a [discursive] mind, the five consciousnesses become the wisdom of accomplishment (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna).
Furthermore, "wisdom of quiescence" is ultimate wisdom (paramārtha-jñāna), while "wisdom of accomplishment" is expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna). Therefore, expedient...

Wisdom responds to the external; true wisdom is in harmony with the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) responds only for a temporary duration, and is therefore called "provisional.
True wisdom, whether responding or not responding, is a single, unchanging wisdom; thus it is called the wisdom of true nature (*svabhāva-jñāna*).
As for this wisdom of nature being non-deluded, it is precisely the mind of *tathatā* (suchness), which has been so from the very beginning.
It is free from the characteristics of names and words; it is free from the characteristics of mental objects. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Only this one fact is real;
the other two are not true. Formerly, a student asked Nanyue: "When a mirror casts an image, once the image has been formed, what then? The Master said: "It does not reflect.
This refers to being deluded regarding the wisdom of the provisional and the ultimate. He further said: "Although it does not..."
The mirror reflects; not even a single point can deceive it. This is none other than original wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The Sixth Patriarch said:
"When seven and six do not arise, five and eight are extinguished. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "All phenomena, from the very beginning, are eternally in the state of quiescent extinction.

Therefore, the sound heard when striking the bamboo and the yellow oriole singing in the willow trees are both not dharmas existing outside the mind; they are solely [the manifestation of the One Mind].
This is the wisdom of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-jñāna*). Therefore, it is not by transforming the *ālayavijñāna* that one achieves the wisdom of perfect nature;

how could this not be believed? Having attained but a slight understanding of the essential gateways of the Chan school, I spent my life seeking outwardly and had not yet returned to the ground of the mind (*citta-bhūmi*).
How then could I have shattered the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of others or severed the deluded state of forgetfulness regarding one's own nature? Now I know...

The dual fusion of nature and characteristics is the non-duality of the ultimate source of wisdom-nature. This is precisely why one must earnestly repent for past errors and wash away all faults and transgressions.
Therefore, I exhort all students of the Way: should you encounter an enlightened teacher, regard them as an ancient Buddha.

If you attain the Dharma through a single word, its benefits will be inexhaustible; you shall transcend vast eons in an instant and proceed directly to Bodhi. If you realize the ground of your own mind...
It is clear that one must necessarily study the teachings and contemplate the mind; only within one's own practice can there be true engagement with them.
If one perceives the Path but does not cultivate it, it is like a person who possesses fertile fields but does not plow them—how could they not regret this themselves?
This is my earnest exhortation.
Relying on the power of my vigor despite my advanced age, though my body is bound by the urgency of illness, I have composed this commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa*.
By means of these superior roots of goodness, may I swiftly behold Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in a future life.
Recorded respectfully by Ji Shi in Han-chuan.
The Elder Yuanfeng has added five-character verses to expand upon the meaning of the eight consciousnesses, totaling sixty-four lines, which are divided into four sections.

△ In the first section, concerning the meaning of the five consciousnesses, there are further two parts: (first, twelve lines of verse on the chapter of ordinary sentiments; second, four lines of verse on the chapter of the fruits of sagehood).
The first verse states:
The five consciousnesses of ordinary sentient beings pervade the eight consciousnesses; internally and externally, they share the same seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).

When perceiving forms and hearing sounds, they function as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in relation to their objective spheres (*viṣaya*). Together with the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*), they correspond simultaneously both internally and externally.
The seeds of the eight consciousnesses and the four afflictions, Contacting objects gives rise to emotional cognition;

Therefore, greed, anger, and delusion are associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, Extending even to the heavens of the Four Formless Realms. It is difficult to exhaustively eliminate these seeds of "self";
next, a verse on the fruits of sainthood:

Where the sound was heard upon striking the bamboo, The nature of consciousness-only was suddenly revealed. Swiftly transforming the five consciousnesses, the seeing and the wisdom become identical within the perfect realm.

[The second section on the intent of the six consciousnesses has two parts: (1) the twelve-line verse on the chapter of ordinary deluded sentiments; (2) the four-line verse on the chapter of the holy fruition.]
The first verse states:
The direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of ordinary beings also involves inference (*anumāna*); that which is established through inference is "with-substantiality" (*sadravya*).

When the object of "with-substantiality" is absent, it is termed a "solitary-image" (*pratibimba*) object. The seeds of the three poisons—self-grasping and craving—impel the activities of the three karmas.
The seeds of the seven consciousnesses and the three natures Perfume and enter the nature of the eighth consciousness;
Together they form the fruits of projecting and completing karma, inexhaustible in their maturation. How painful! Great beings, The suffering of saṃsāra is not yet exhausted.
Next, the verse on the holy fruit:
Suddenly shattering the seeds of ignorance, one penetrates the nature of consciousness-only. Within the wisdom of wondrous observation, the reflection of capacities never ceases.

[The third section, concerning the purport of the seven consciousnesses, has two parts: first, a verse of twelve lines on the chapter of ordinary sentiments; second, a verse of four lines on the chapter of the holy fruit.]
The first verse states:

The ordinary mind and the seven consciousnesses grasp the eighth consciousness; it is of the nature of obscured-neutral. It possesses a substantial essence and penetrates both the phenomenal and the fundamental, taking the grasping of self as its object.
The emotional consciousnesses penetrate both the internal and external, hooking together the shadows of the six sense objects.
Even up to the four heavens of the formless realm, as long as the seeds of my views are not exhausted, by the power of this meditative concentration,
the fetters and latent tendencies shall not remain; therefore, when the celestial retribution is exhausted, one returns to the well of the eightfold cycle of rebirth,
whereupon the fruits of sainthood are attained in succession.
Suddenly shattering the seeds of deluded nature, Pure wisdom is free from the nature of birth; In the equal and pure *dharmadhātu*, there is neither Buddha nor the nature of birth.

[Within the exposition of the four divisions and eight consciousnesses, there are further two parts: first, the twelve-line verse on the chapter of ordinary sentiments; second, the four-line verse on the chapter of the holy fruit.]
The first verse states:
The ordinary mind is the eighth, the *ālayavijñāna*, which is associated with the seeds of the four afflictions.
Within the stage of an Arhat, these four afflictions are finally and completely relinquished; therefore, the Sūtra says that there are three natures and three non-natures.
The imaginary is non-existent; the dependent is the perfected. The perfected is the meaning of liberation, like space and the six unconditioned phenomena.
These reveal the characteristics of all dharmas, which are all of an immovable nature.
Next, the verse on the untainted:
Within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, The seeds of latent tendencies are entirely liberated; This is named the Stainless Consciousness, Which illuminates the reflections of the great trichiliocosm.
[This concludes the summary verse on the names and numbers of the eight consciousnesses.]
In the six desire realms, all eight consciousnesses are present; In the first and second dhyānas, there are six consciousnesses;
In the third dhyāna, three consciousnesses are present; in the fourth dhyāna, only seven or eight. In the four formless attainments, the ālayavijñāna exists.

As the various consciousnesses are about to cease, The desire realm possesses both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); In the second dhyāna, vicāra has not yet subsided; In the third dhyāna, vicāra is about to be severed.
In the four dhyānas there is no *vicāra* (investigation) at all;

in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) all three are present: food, sleep, and sexual desire. In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), these are all abandoned, and one takes only meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) as desire.
In the fourth dhyāna, there are the universal mental factors: attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).
The seven consciousnesses are characterized by grasping; the eighth consciousness is of the nature of obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). In the four formless heavens, it is non-obscured (*anivṛta*);
it possesses only the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the five universal mental factors. The nine successive attainments have already ceased in the stage of the Arhat.
Suddenly shattering the synthetic consciousness, Only the Great Perfect Wisdom remains, Universally illuminating all lands and moments, encompassing all.

[Verse on the General Meaning of the Transformation of the Eight Consciousnesses into Wisdom] The eight consciousnesses can be divided into the five sensory cognitions; The mental factors are perfectly accomplished, manifesting as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In a single instant, it flows into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*);
within the domain of inference, it appears as a solitary reflection, resembling reality through two aspects that carry both the general and the particular.
If the *ālayavijñāna*, whether obscured or unobscured, can suddenly shatter the seeds of ignorance, the light of the wisdom of intrinsic nature will always be present before one’s face.

If one is in the realm of the fourth dhyāna, within the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*), it has already ceased. Therefore, it is established as such.

This is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). It is merely subsumed under the nature of imagined construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); it does not belong to the essence of the fundamental nature (*dharmatā-svabhāva*), for it constitutes the phenomena of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Second, regarding the unconditioned phenomenon of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): it refers to the cessation of phenomena such as arising and ceasing, coming and going, good and evil, as well as the aforementioned space (*ākāśa*).
As for the "object" (*viṣaya*): because it is non-associated (*viprayukta*). Why? Because it is not that which is seen by the mind, intellect, or consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).

Rather, from the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) through the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and the four fruits (*catuḥ-phala*), up to the stage of the Tathāgata, its essence is the fundamental self-nature (*mūla-svabhāva*).

Therefore, it is called the unconditioned dharma of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta-dharma*). Among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the essence of the sages (*ārya*).
This is the Dharma. Furthermore, the former refers to the meaning of falsity; the latter refers to the meaning of true nature.

Third, regarding the unconditioned state of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): this refers to the nine successive absorptions of the Hīnayāna, so called because it extinguishes the mind, intellect, and consciousness.

Therefore, it belongs to the category of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The three vehicles (*triyāna*) traverse *samādhi*; this may also be cultivated by borrowing the path, but it is not the Dharma of the supreme vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).

Fourth, as for cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned, it refers to the immeasurable supramundane sublime practices such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Question: Since there are those who cultivate morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), it cannot be accomplished without employing a mind subject to arising and ceasing.

How, then, can these be categorized as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)? Answer: It is because one employs morality, concentration, and wisdom to discern and eliminate the dharma of cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Thus, one is able to select and remove the seeds of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), extinguishing all afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their latent tendencies (*anuśaya-bīja*). Only then does one first perceive the Truth.

It is like the wondrous fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, it is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because it belongs to the category of unconditioned phenomena. Question:

Within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), to which nature does it belong? Answer: It belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The five types of unconditioned *tathatā* (true suchness) comprise the previously mentioned space and the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), as well as the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) within the gate of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, they include the previously mentioned unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which belongs to the gate of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Because these two gates are inseparable from one another, they are called the gate of *tathatā*. As for the gate of *tathatā*, it encompasses the mundane and supramundane, and so forth.
All phenomena are, in their totality, nothing other than the single mind. Therefore, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"Whatever one perceives as all phenomena is merely the mind alone. Question: Among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), under which nature is this subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed equally within all three natures and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).
The six immovable unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are also the collective meaning of the five unconditioned phenomena; here they are specifically referred to by the term "immovable.
This is precisely the stage of the Tathāgata’s fruition, which is of vajra-nature; therefore, it is called the meaning of the immovable.

Now, as for the dharmas of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), they are simply the single nature alone. Why, then, must six dharmas of non-action be established? Answer: It is because one distinguishes between essence (*tī*) and function (*yòng*).
Furthermore, it is out of fear that [the Buddhist view] might be confused with the views of external paths (*tīrthika*).

While directly pointing to the single mind, it is also shown that the essence and function of True Suchness (*tathatā*) are fully present, for it is eternally unmoving. For these reasons, the six dharmas of non-action are established.
He asked again: "Why is it necessary to establish that space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? He replied:
"It is because the nature of space is discerned through selection and is not its inherent nature (*prakṛti*). Space is that which is perceived by our mind, intellect, and consciousness;
inherent nature is that which is not perceived by the mind, intellect, and consciousness. Although inherent nature is empty, it is not severed; therefore, it is not inert."
It is merely empty.
Question: Why is it necessary to establish the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? Answer:

Because it reveals that both ordinary beings and noble ones alike rely upon the fundamental self-nature, which is dissociated from all defiled phenomena; therefore, it belongs exclusively to the essence of ordinary beings and noble ones.
Question: Why must the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) be established as unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)? Answer:
Did we not say previously that all three vehicles borrow this path for their practice, and are likewise able to sever the seeds of self-love?
Question: Why must the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) be established? Answer:
It is because, through the power of the sublime function of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation, one is able to transform ordinary states of mind and attain the stage of a sage (*ārya*).
If this analytical cessation did not exist, the fruits of all saintly attainments and their virtuous stages could not be accomplished.

Question: Why is it necessary to establish *tathatā* (suchness) as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Answer: Because it subsumes the essence and function of the preceding four kinds of unconditioned phenomena within a single suchness;
and because it directly reveals that the one mind is devoid of dualistic dharmas.
Question: Why is it necessary to establish the unconditioned state of immovability (*aniñjya-asamskṛta*)? Answer:

Because that which subsumes the preceding five kinds of unconditioned phenomena is by nature like a diamond (*vajra*); since the mind is without movement, it eternally abides in the *dharmadhātu*, being without change or transformation.
For this reason, the name "immovable" is established. Furthermore, regarding these six unconditioned phenomena, that which is one unconditioned phenomenon is itself the six unconditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, space and the unconditioned state of cessation (*nirodha-asamskṛta*) constitute the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena (*dharmadhātu-avighna*).

The unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*) constitutes the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of principle (*dharmadhātu-artha*). True Suchness (*tathatā-asamskṛta*) constitutes the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomenon and principle (*dharmadhātu-artha-vighna*).
The unconditioned state of immovability (*aniñjya-asamskṛta*) encompasses the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadhātu-dharmāvighna*).
Furthermore, it is said that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) can be known by means of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Why is this?

It has been heard in the sacred scriptures that there are six paths of the unconditioned. Because these were cultivated into seeds during former lives, when one hears of the six paths of the unconditioned today, they manifest as existing.
Thus, the path of the unconditioned cannot be known [directly].
It is known. How much more so can it be known by consciousness? Therefore it is said: "The Way may be called the Way, yet it is not that there is a name for a permanent Way.
There is nothing that is not temporarily called the Way. Now, to take consciousness alone and to cognize the unconditioned Way—this is the object-condition (ālambana-viṣaya) for us human beings.
Yet this object is such that by taking the absence of an object as the object, it first becomes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
This is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Therefore, this realm is neither great nor small; it is neither internal nor external;

it is not an object of inference (*anumāna*), nor is it attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus the Sage said: "Only when one encounters the realm with a mind free from attachment can one begin to realize the Way."

(By Yuan Zhang) When I first began my studies, the poisonous influence of the "self-nature" demon nearly destroyed my life of wisdom; the suffering was beyond description.
Arriving here in the south, I was fortunate to encounter my late teacher, the Venerable Yuanfeng, who bestowed upon me the nectar of the Dharma, reviving me after I had been dead and gone.

Consequently, I have made a great vow: that throughout all future ages, for as many beings as there are, I shall universally manifest form-bodies, possess all wondrous eloquence, and extensively praise the One Vehicle, so that all sentient beings may not fall into false views.

Having come to hear the Dharma, I rejoice in the bliss of the Dharma and the understanding of the Dharma; seeing no urgent worldly affairs whatsoever, I only wish to propagate the Dharma for the universal benefit of all living beings.

It was at such a time that this treatise was composed. With the six sense-faculties purified and the single nature perfectly enlightened, may the flames of wisdom regarding non-arising blaze forth in successive layers.
I reverently pray that the Protectors of the Dharma will first grant their protection, so that the Buddha’s [teachings] may...
The Dharma shall abide long in the world, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings;
every word and every phrase, down to a single speck of dust or a drop of ink, accords with reality and pervades the entirety of the *sāhasra-lokadhātus* throughout the future.
Within all sentient beings, every word and every phrase accords with reality, encompassing all beings so that they all enter therein.
May all sentient beings awaken to the Dharma-gate of self-nature, wherein phenomena naturally interact without obstruction—this is the proof of this treatise.
May all who relinquish wealth to provide assistance, who exert a single effort of sympathetic joy, and who offer praise, never fall into the three miserable realms throughout their successive lives;
may they always encounter humans and devas, hear the True Dharma, attain great *dhāraṇī*, and universally transform and enlighten all.

It is because they cause sentient beings to equally perfect the knowledge of all modes, universally encompassing them as sentient beings through the compassionate vow, by means of correct deliverance,
and because there is no distinction among the three [bodies].
